lessons.title: What money is for

flow.q: Put €100 in a drawer. Today a coffee at the café costs €1. Twenty years from now, say, it costs €2. How many coffees can you buy with that €100 in twenty years?
flow.after: Today €100 buys you 100 coffees. If the price doubles, the same €100 buys **50**. The banknote in the drawer hasn't changed: what you can do with it has. Money does three jobs, and this is the most delicate one.

flow.x:
**Money in itself is worth nothing: it is worth what it lets you do.**

It does three different jobs.

• **Medium of exchange.** You hand it over in exchange for what you need. Without money you would have to barter: a baker who wants a pair of shoes would have to find a shoemaker who wants bread.
• **Unit of account.** It is the yardstick for measuring prices. A coffee costs €1.30, a book €18: you can compare them because they use the same measure.
• **Store of value.** It lets you move value through time: you earn today, you spend tomorrow.

You see the first two jobs every day, when you pay and when you look at a price. The third only shows over the years.

items: You pay for groceries at the checkout
You give money in exchange for things: that is exchange.
You compare the price of two phones
You use money as a yardstick for measuring.
You set aside €200 for a vacation
You move value from today to tomorrow.
You receive your salary for your work
You trade your work for money.
You read that a car costs €15,000
A price is a measurement expressed in money.
You keep €1,000 in your account for emergencies
You save it to use later.

flow.x:
Of the three jobs, the third is the one money does worst.

As a medium of exchange and as a unit of account, money always works. As a store of value it has an enemy: rising prices.

Go back to the €100 in the drawer.

[fig]

After twenty years the banknote is the same, but it buys half as much. Keeping money idle looks like the safest choice, because the figure never goes down. In reality it is a slow loss that you can't see.

Everything else in this path starts from here. **Interest** and **investments** exist for this reason: so that the money you set aside doesn't lose ground and, if possible, gains some.

rows.lab: In twenty years, with coffee at €2

lessons.note: Money is for paying, for measuring prices and for storing value. The third job is the most fragile: if prices rise, idle money buys less.

ex.q: You put €500 in a drawer to buy a bike a year from now. Which job are you asking of the money?
ex.exp: You are keeping it to spend later: that is the **store of value** function. It will become a medium of exchange only on the day you pay for the bike.

ex.q: Why isn't money kept in a drawer for many years a perfect store of value?
options: Because if prices rise it buys fewer things
ex.exp: The figure stays the same, but if prices rise in the meantime, that figure buys **fewer things**. Banknotes don't expire, and the bank has nothing to do with a drawer.

lessons.title: Simple interest

flow.q: You lend a friend €1,000 for 3 years. You agree on this: each year they pay you 5% of the amount lent, and at the end they give you back the €1,000. How much extra do you collect in all?
flow.after: 5% of €1,000 is €50 a year. Over three years: \(50 \times 3 =\) **€150**. That payment has a name, interest, and the way you calculated it is called simple interest.

flow.x:
**When you lend money, you give up using it for a while. Interest is the payment for giving it up.**

When you lend someone €1,000, for the whole length of the loan that money is not available to you, and you run the risk that it won't come back. In exchange you ask for a payment: **interest**.

Interest is measured with a **rate**: a percentage of the amount lent, usually per year. A rate of 5% a year means €5 of interest for every €100 lent, for every year.

The amount lent is called the **principal**.

It works both ways. When you deposit money in a bank, you are the one lending, and you receive the interest. When you take out a loan, you pay it.

With **simple interest** the rate is always applied only to the starting principal. That is why the interest is the same every year.

Here is the €1,000 lent at 5% a year for 3 years:

[fig]

At the end you have \(1{,}000 + 150 =\) **€1,150**. The total at the end, principal plus interest, is called the **final amount**.

The calculation can be written in one line:

$$I = C \times i \times t$$

Where \(I\) is the interest, \(C\) the principal, \(i\) the annual rate and \(t\) the number of years. Here: \(1{,}000 \times 5\% \times 3 = \text{€}150\).

fig.cap: Three equal pieces of interest, because they are always calculated on the starting €1,000.

flow.q: You lend €2,000 at 3% a year, at simple interest. How much interest do you earn in one year?
flow.exp: \(2{,}000 \times 3\% =\) **€60**. With simple interest it will be €60 in the second year too, in the third and in every other.

flow.q: Same loan: €2,000 at 3% a year, simple interest, for 4 years. What is the final amount?
flow.exp: Interest: €60 a year for 4 years, \(60 \times 4 = \text{€}240\). Final amount: \(2{,}000 + 240 =\) **€2,240**.

lessons.note: Simple interest: \(\text{principal} \times \text{rate} \times \text{years}\). The interest is the same every year.

pairs: Interest as a percentage, for one year

ex.q: You deposit €5,000 at 2% a year, simple interest, for 3 years. How much interest do you earn in all?
ex.exp: Each year: \(5{,}000 \times 2\% = \text{€}100\). In 3 years: \(100 \times 3 =\) **€300**. The answer €100 is just one year; €306 is what compound interest would give, which we see in the next lesson.

ex.q: What does a rate of 4% a year tell you?
options: That each year the interest is €4 for every €100 of principal
That €4 in all is paid back at the end
ex.exp: The rate is the interest as a percentage of the principal, for one year: at 4%, **€4 for every €100, every year**. On €1,000 that is €40 a year.

lessons.title: Compound interest

flow.q: You put €1,000 at 5% a year and leave it untouched for 30 years. Each year the interest stays in and earns interest too. How much do you have at the end?
flow.after: With simple interest you would have \(1{,}000 + 50 \times 30 = \text{€}2{,}500\). Letting the interest work too gets you to about **€4,322**. The difference, more than €1,800, is interest earned on interest.

flow.x:
**With compound interest the interest doesn't sit aside: it is added to the principal and starts earning too.**

You start with €1,000 at 5% a year.

• **Year 1**: \(5\% \times 1{,}000 = \text{€}50\). You have €1,050.
• **Year 2**: the 5% is calculated on €1,050, no longer on €1,000. That is €52.50. You have €1,102.50.
• **Year 3**: \(5\% \times 1{,}102.50 = \text{€}55.13\). You have €1,157.63.

[fig]

Each year the interest is a little higher than the year before, because it is calculated on a figure that keeps growing. At first the difference from simple interest is small. As time goes by it becomes enormous.
Move the years slider. The columns show three pieces: your money, the interest on your money and the interest on the interest. Watch which of the three grows the most as the years go up.

flow.t: Time matters more than the amount
flow.x:
After \(t\) years at rate \(i\), the principal \(C\) becomes:

$$M = C \times (1 + i)^t$$

At 5%, each year the amount is multiplied by 1.05. After two years you have multiplied it twice, after thirty years thirty times.

Here is €1,000 at 5% a year, with simple and with compound interest:

| After | Simple | Compound |
|---|---|---|
| 1 year | €1,050 | €1,050 |
| 10 years | €1,500 | €1,629 |
| 20 years | €2,000 | €2,653 |
| 30 years | €2,500 | €4,322 |

In the first years the two columns almost coincide. Then the one on the right runs away. That is why someone who starts early with a little often ends up ahead of someone who starts late with a lot.

flow.q: You put €2,000 at 10% a year with compound interest. How much do you have after 2 years?
flow.exp: First year: \(2{,}000 \times 1.10 = \text{€}2{,}200\). Second year: \(2{,}200 \times 1.10 =\) **€2,420**. With simple interest you would be at €2,400: the extra €20 is the interest earned on the first year's interest.

lessons.note: Time matters more than the starting amount: interest on interest grows slowly at first and fast later.

ex.q: You put €1,000 at 5% a year. How much do you have after 2 years?
ex.exp: In the first year you reach €1,050. In the second year the 5% is calculated on €1,050: that is €52.50, not 50. Total **€1,102.50**. Anyone who answers €1,100 counted the 5% twice on the starting €1,000.

ex.q: You put €2,000 at 4% a year with compound interest. How much do you have after 3 years?
ex.exp:
| Year | Calculation | End of year |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | \(2{,}000.00 \times 1.04\) | 2,080.00 |
| 2 | \(2{,}080.00 \times 1.04\) | 2,163.20 |
| 3 | \(2{,}163.20 \times 1.04\) | 2,249.73 |

The typical mistake is counting the 4% each year on the starting €2,000: that gets you to €2,240.

lessons.title: Inflation

flow.q: You have €1,000 sitting in a drawer. Prices rise 3% a year. In 10 years, how much do those €1,000 buy, measured at today's prices?
flow.after: In ten years, what costs €1,000 today will cost about €1,344. So your €1,000 will buy what you can buy today with about **€744**. The figure in the drawer is the same: it is its value that has dropped by a quarter.

flow.x:
**Inflation is a general rise in prices over time.**

General means it isn't about a single product. If only the price of peaches goes up because the harvest was bad, that isn't inflation. It is when, on average, the cost of everything a household buys goes up: food, bills, rent, transport.

It is measured as a percentage per year. Inflation of 3% means that what costs €100 today will cost €103 on average a year from now.

To measure it you use a **basket**: a list of goods and services that stands for what households typically spend on. Every month someone checks how much it costs to fill it and compares that with a year earlier.

What matters about your money is not the figure, but what you can buy with it. This is called **purchasing power**.

When prices rise and your figure stays the same, purchasing power falls. Here are the €1,000 from the drawer, with inflation at 3% a year:

[fig]

There are still €1,000 in the drawer. Nobody has taken them. Yet after ten years it is as if you had €744, and after twenty €554.

That is why keeping everything idle is not a risk-free choice: it is the choice of losing a little at a time, with certainty.

fig.cap: With inflation at 3% a year, measuring everything at today's prices.

flow.x: You have €1,000 sitting idle. Move inflation and years and see how much they buy, at today's prices.

goals.label: Find when €1,000 buys less than €750
goals.hint: You can raise inflation, or let more years pass.

goals.label: Now halve purchasing power with inflation at 2%
goals.hint: Bring inflation back to 2% and add years: it takes a long time.

flow.after: Even low inflation, left to work for decades, halves the value of idle money. At 2% it takes about 35 years, at 6% just 12.

flow.q: Your weekly grocery shopping costs €200 today. With inflation of 5%, how much will the same shopping cost in a year?
flow.exp: \(200 \times 1.05 =\) **€210**: €10 more to buy the same things.

lessons.note: With inflation, idle money loses purchasing power, even if the figure in the account doesn't fall.

ex.q: Inflation is 3% a year and your account earns 1%. After a year, what has happened to your purchasing power?
ex.exp: The account grew by 1%, but prices by 3%: in real terms you lost about **2%** (to be precise, \(\dfrac{1.01}{1.03} - 1 = -1.94\%\)).

ex.q: What does inflation measure?
options: The average rise in the prices of everything households buy
The rise in the price of a single product
How much a bank account earns
ex.exp: Inflation looks at prices as a whole, through a basket of goods and services. If one product goes up and the rest stay put, that is not inflation.

lessons.title: Real rate

flow.q: Bank A offers you 2% a year at a time when prices rise 1%. Bank B offers you 5% at a time when prices rise 6%. In which case can you buy more at the end of the year than before?
flow.after: With A your money grows 2% and prices 1%: in the end you can buy about 1% more. With B it grows 5%, but prices grow 6%: you can buy about 1% less, even though you see a higher figure in your account. What counts is the rate once inflation is taken out: it is called the real rate.

flow.x:
**An interest rate alone doesn't tell you whether you are gaining: you have to compare it with inflation.**

The rate you read on the contract is called the **nominal rate**: it says by how much the figure grows.

The **real rate** says instead by how much your purchasing power grows, that is, what you can buy. It is the nominal rate cleaned of inflation.

For everyday calculations a subtraction is enough:

$$\text{real} \approx \text{nominal} - \text{inflation}$$

[fig]

If the real rate is positive, at the end of the year you can buy more. If it is negative you can buy less, even if the figure in the account has gone up.

fig.cap: With A the rate beats prices: real about +1%. With B your money loses: real about −1%.

flow.x:
The subtraction is a good approximation. The precise calculation divides instead of subtracting:

$$1 + r = \frac{1 + n}{1 + \pi}$$

Where \(r\) is the real rate, \(n\) the nominal rate and \(\pi\) inflation.

With a nominal rate of 5% and inflation of 2%:

• approximate: \(5\% - 2\% =\) **3%**
• exact: \(\dfrac{1.05}{1.02} - 1 =\) **2.94%**

Why divide? In a year €100 becomes €105, but what cost €100 now costs €102. With €105 you buy \(\dfrac{105}{102} = 1.0294\) times what you bought before.

With low rates the two calculations almost coincide. The higher the rates, the wider the gap.

flow.q: A savings account earns 3.5% a year and inflation is 2%. Roughly what is the real rate? Use subtraction.

flow.t: Does your purchasing power go up or down?
items: Rate 4%, inflation 1%
Rate 2%, inflation 5%
Rate 0%, inflation 2%
Idle money loses about 2% a year.
Rate 6%, inflation 3%
Rate 7%, inflation 9%
A high rate isn't enough if inflation is higher.
Rate 1%, inflation 0%
Without inflation the whole rate is real gain.

lessons.note: \(\text{Real rate} \approx \text{nominal} - \text{inflation}\). If the real rate is negative, you are losing purchasing power.

ex.q: An investment earns 4% a year and inflation is 6%. Roughly what is the real rate?
ex.exp: \(\text{Real} \approx 4\% - 6\% =\) **−2%**. The investment pays you, but less than prices are rising: in real terms you lose.

ex.q: Your salary rises 3% in a year when prices rise 3%. What has happened to what you can buy?
ex.exp: Salary and prices rose at the same pace: your purchasing power stayed **where it was**. The same reasoning as the real rate applies to salaries, rents and pensions.

lessons.title: Stocks

pages.x:
A **stock** is an ownership stake in a company. If the company has issued 1,000 shares and you own 10, you own 1% of it.

Whoever owns stocks earns in two ways:

• the **dividend**, that is the part of profit the company distributes to its owners;
• the rise in the **price**, if the stock is worth more when you resell it.

Neither the dividend nor the price is guaranteed. If the company does badly, the dividend can disappear and the price can fall.

In exchange for this risk, over the long run stocks have returned more on average than bonds.

lessons.note: Stock = an ownership stake. It pays through dividends and price growth, with no guarantees.

ex.q: A company has 2,000 shares outstanding and you own 50. What portion of the company is yours?

lessons.title: Bonds

pages.x:
A **bond** is a loan you make to a company or a government. In exchange you receive:

• a **coupon**, that is the interest paid at fixed dates;
• the **redemption** of the principal at maturity.

A 10-year BTP (an Italian government bond) with a 3% coupon on €1,000 pays you €30 a year and gives you back €1,000 after 10 years.

lessons.note: Bond = loan. Fixed coupons and redemption at maturity; the price falls when rates rise.

pairs: An ownership stake in a company
A loan to a company or a government
The part of profit paid to the owners

ex.q: Interest rates fall. What usually happens to the price of bonds already in circulation?
ex.exp: Bonds already issued pay higher coupons than new ones, so they are worth more: the price **rises**. Interest rates and bond prices move in opposite directions.

lessons.title: Funds and ETFs

pages.x:
A **mutual fund** pools the money of many savers and invests it in many securities together. You don't buy individual stocks or bonds: you buy **shares** of the fund.

The value of one share is calculated like this:

$$\text{share value} = \frac{\text{net assets}}{\text{number of shares}}$$

If the fund has net assets of €10 million divided into 1 million shares, each share is worth **€10**. With €500 you buy 50.

An **ETF** is a fund that is bought and sold on the stock market like a stock and that usually **tracks an index**, that is a basket of securities chosen by a fixed rule (for example the 500 largest US companies).

• An **active** fund has a manager who picks the securities and costs more, often between 1% and 2% a year.
• An ETF that tracks an index doesn't pick anything and costs less, often between 0.1% and 0.3% a year.

In both cases you hold many different securities with a single transaction.

lessons.note: A fund pools the money of many people and buys many securities. An ETF is a fund listed on the stock market that tracks an index and costs little.

ex.q: A fund has net assets of €50 million divided into 2 million shares. How much is one share worth?
What does an ETF that tracks an index do?
options: It picks the best securities every day
It buys the index's securities, without picking
ex.exp: It buys the securities that make up the index, in the same proportions, **without picking**. That is why it costs little. It doesn't guarantee the principal: if the index falls, the ETF falls too.

lessons.title: Accounts, deposits and liquidity

pages.x:
• The **checking account** is for receiving and paying. It earns little or nothing.
• The **deposit account** is made for leaving a sum untouched: in exchange the bank pays you interest. The money is often **locked**: if you withdraw it before maturity you lose the interest, in whole or in part, and in some cases you can't withdraw it at all.

Example: €5,000 in a deposit account at 3% for a year earns \(5{,}000 \times 3\% =\) **€150** before taxes. In Italy the tax on interest is 26%: you keep **€111**.

**Liquidity** means how quickly you can turn something into cash without losing money. A checking account is extremely liquid. A house is not: selling it takes months.

For the unexpected you need an **emergency fund**: liquid money equal to a few months of expenses. A common rule is to keep 3 to 6 months.

If you spend €1,500 a month, the emergency fund goes from €4,500 to €9,000. Only what is left over makes sense to invest.

lessons.note: Money you may need soon sits in liquid instruments. The rest can work over longer periods.

ex.q: You spend €1,200 a month and want an emergency fund that covers 4 months. How much do you need to set aside?
ex.exp: \(1{,}200 \times 4 =\) **€4,800**. €14,400 would be a whole year of expenses.

lessons.title: Risk and return

pages.x:
Nobody pays you more without asking for something in return. A higher expected return always comes with more **risk**, that is with results that can stray far from the average, up and down.

If someone promises high returns with no risk, a piece of the story is missing.

pages.t: Not all your eggs in one basket
pages.x:
To **diversify** means to split your money among many different securities. If one does badly, it weighs little on the total.

Diversification doesn't remove all the risk: the risk tied to the whole market remains. It removes the risk of betting everything on the wrong company.

lessons.note: More expected return, more risk. Diversifying reduces the risk of individual companies, not that of the market.

ex.q: All your savings are in the stock of a single company. What is the most direct way to reduce the risk?
options: Buy more stock of the same company
Split the money among many different companies
ex.exp: Splitting the money among many companies is how you **diversify**: the trouble of a single one weighs little on the total.

lessons.title: Diversifying with numbers

pages.x:
Take two companies that react in opposite ways to the same news. Company A gains when oil rises, company B when it falls.

| Scenario | A | B | Half and half |
|---|---|---|---|
| Oil up | +20% | −5% | +7.5% |
| Oil down | −10% | +15% | +2.5% |

With all the money on A the result ranges from +20% to −10%. With half on A and half on B it ranges from +7.5% to +2.5%: same world, far fewer surprises.

A portfolio's return is the average of the securities' returns, weighted by how much you put in each:

$$R_p = w_A \times R_A + w_B \times R_B$$

Where \(R_p\) is the portfolio's return, \(w_A\) and \(w_B\) are the fractions put in the two securities, which add up to 1, and \(R_A\) and \(R_B\) are their returns.

Oil up: \(0.5 \times 20\% + 0.5 \times (-5\%) =\) **+7.5%**.

Diversification works when the securities **don't all move together**. Ten companies in the same sector diversify little.

lessons.note: Combining securities that don't move the same way reduces the swings of the portfolio.

ex.q: You have 60% in a security that returns +10% and 40% in a security that returns −5%. What does the portfolio return?
ex.exp: \(0.6 \times 10\% + 0.4 \times (-5\%) = 6\% - 2\% =\) **+4%**. The +2.5% would be the simple average, right only with half and half.

lessons.title: The time horizon

pages.x:
The **time horizon** is the time that passes before you need that money. It is the first question to ask, even before choosing the instrument.

• Money you need **within a year or two**, like the down payment on a house: liquid, stable instruments.
• Money you need **in ten years or more**, like retirement: it can sit in instruments that swing, because there is time to recover.

pages.t: Why a loss weighs more than it seems
pages.x:
If an investment drops 30%, to get back to the starting point a +30% is not enough.

Start with €100. After a −30% you have €70. To get back to €100 you need €30 on €70, that is a **+42.9%**.

$$\text{recovery} = \frac{1}{1 - \text{loss}} - 1$$

With a 50% loss the recovery needed is **100%**: the money has to double. That is why someone with little time ahead can't afford big swings.

lessons.note: The later you need the money, the more swings you can bear. A loss always demands a bigger recovery in percentage terms.

ex.q: An investment loses 50%. By how much must it rise to get back to its starting value?
ex.exp: From €100 you drop to €50. To get back to €100 the €50 has to double: **+100%**.

ex.q: You need €20,000 in eight months for the down payment on a house. Where does it make the most sense to keep it?
options: In stocks, to make it grow
In a fund that invests in a single sector
ex.exp: Eight months is a short horizon: if stocks fall you don't have time to recover. You need **liquid, stable** instruments.

lessons.title: Costs

pages.x:
Every instrument has a cost: management fees, purchase fees, sale fees. They look like small numbers because they are expressed as a percentage per year, but they are paid **every year** and on the **total** invested, not only on the gains.

The return before costs is called **gross**, what is left to you is **net**:

$$\text{net} \approx \text{gross} - \text{costs}$$

A fund that returns 5% before costs and costs 1.5% a year leaves you about **3.5%**.

You invest €10,000 for 30 years in two instruments that both return 6% a year before costs. The first costs 0.2% a year, the second 2%. Assumptions: no other contributions, costs taken out every year.

| Annual cost | Net | After 30 years |
|---|---|---|
| 0.2% | 5.8% | €54,271 |
| 2.0% | 4.0% | €32,434 |

The difference is about **€21,800**, more than double the amount invested. It is compound interest working in reverse: costs take out money that would have kept earning.

lessons.note: Costs are paid every year and compound like interest. All else equal, the instrument that costs less leaves you more.

ex.q: A fund returns 7% a year before costs and costs 1.8% a year. About how much is left to you?
ex.exp: \(7\% - 1.8\% =\) about **5.2%**. Costs are taken off the return, not added to it.

lessons.title: How a loan works

flow.q: You need €3,310 for a used motorcycle. The bank lends it to you at 10% a year and you repay it in 3 equal yearly installments. How much interest do you pay it in total?
flow.after: Many people say €993, that is 10% of €3,310 for three years. But each installment also pays back a piece of the debt, so interest is calculated on a figure that goes down. In all it is **€683**: now let's see where it comes from.

flow.x:
**Taking out a loan means using money today that you don't have, and paying it back a little at a time.**

The bank gives you the €3,310 for the motorcycle right away: that amount is called the **principal**.

But the bank doesn't do it for free. For every year you hold its money it asks for a payment, the **interest**: here 10% of what you still owe it.

Each year you pay a fixed amount, the **installment**: €1,331. Inside it are two different things:

• one part pays the interest for that year;
• the rest pays back a piece of the principal.

[fig]

The more principal you repay, the less you owe the bank, and the less interest you will pay the following year.

fig.cap: What each piece is worth changes from year to year: we see it next.

flow.x:
Let's work out the first installment.

At the start you owe the bank the whole €3,310. The interest for the first year is 10% of that amount:

• Interest: \(10\% \times 3{,}310 =\) **€331**

The installment is €1,331. Take out the interest, and what is left pays back principal:

• Principal repaid: \(1{,}331 - 331 =\) **€1,000**

[fig]

After the first installment you no longer owe €3,310, but \(3{,}310 - 1{,}000 =\) **€2,310**. Next year's interest is calculated on this figure, which is lower.

flow.q:
Second year. Now you owe the bank €2,310, and the rate is still 10%.

| Year | Interest | Principal | Balance |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 331 | 1,000 | 2,310 |
| 2 | **?** | | |

How much interest do you pay in the second year?
flow.exp: \(10\% \times 2{,}310 =\) **€231**. The rest of the installment, \(1{,}331 - 231 = \text{€}1{,}100\), pays back principal: the debt falls to €1,210.

flow.q:
Third year. You have €1,210 of debt left at 10%, and the installment is still €1,331.

| Year | Interest | Principal | Balance |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 331 | 1,000 | 2,310 |
| 2 | 231 | 1,100 | 1,210 |
| 3 | 121 | **?** | |

How much principal do you repay with the last installment?
flow.exp: Interest: \(10\% \times 1{,}210 = \text{€}121\). Principal repaid: \(1{,}331 - 121 =\) **€1,210**, which is all the debt that was left. The loan is paid off.

flow.t: The installment stays the same, the inside changes
flow.x:
Here are the three installments one under the other. The amount is always €1,331, but look at how the inside changes.

[fig]

Year after year the debt goes down, so the interest goes down and the part that repays principal grows.

And the €683 from the opening question? It is the interest of the three installments added together: \(331 + 231 + 121 =\) **€683**. It is the price you pay for having the motorcycle right away.

For the curious, the equal installment that makes the numbers work is found like this:

$$R = C \times \frac{i}{1 - (1 + i)^{-n}}$$

Where \(R\) is the installment, \(C\) the principal, \(i\) the rate per period and \(n\) the number of installments.

flow.t: As the years go by, does it go up or down?
items: The interest portion
Interest is calculated on the debt that is left, and the debt shrinks with every installment.
The installment
In this type of loan the installment is the same from the first to the last.
The principal portion
The installment is fixed and the interest goes down: what is left over to reduce the debt grows.
The remaining balance
Each installment pays back a piece of it.

lessons.note: The installment stays the same, but its inside changes: more interest at first, then almost only principal.

ex.q: You borrow €5,000 at 8% a year. How much interest accrues in the first year?
ex.exp: \(5{,}000 \times 8\% =\) **€400**. In the following years the interest goes down, because the remaining balance shrinks.

ex.q: In a loan with a constant installment, how does the first installment compare with the last?
options: It has less interest and more principal
It is the same inside too
It has more interest and less principal
ex.exp: At the start the debt is at its highest, so interest weighs more and there is less room for principal. In the lesson's example the first installment has €331 of interest, the last €121.

lessons.title: Interest rate and APR

flow.q: Two banks offer you the same loan: same amount, same term. Bank A asks for a rate of 5%, bank B 6%. Which costs you less?
flow.after: The rate alone is not enough: the **fees** are missing. A loan at 5% with high fees can cost more than one at 6% with no fees. That is why every loan has two numbers: the nominal interest rate and the APR.

flow.t: The rate doesn't tell the whole story
flow.x:
When you take out a loan you pay two kinds of costs.

The first is **interest**, the payment to the bank for the money it lends you. The rate that measures it is called the **nominal interest rate**.

The second is **fees**: setting up the loan, collecting each payment, sometimes insurance the bank requires you to take out. They are not in the nominal rate.

That is why there is a second number, the **APR**, the annual percentage rate: it puts interest and mandatory fees together and tells you how much the loan really costs in a year.

[fig]

When you compare two offers, look at the APR.

rows.lab: How much a loan costs you
segs: Interest: measured by the nominal rate

fig.cap: The APR measures the whole bar, the nominal rate only the first piece.

flow.t: Does it count in the APR?
items: Interest on the loan
Interest is the first piece of the APR: it is what the nominal rate measures.
Loan processing fees
They are mandatory fees for getting the loan: they count.
Fees for collecting each payment
You pay them with every installment and can't avoid them: they count.
Mandatory insurance
If you can't get the loan without the policy, its cost counts.
Optional insurance
If you can get the loan without it, it isn't a mandatory cost: it stays out.
Late-payment interest (for those who pay late)
You pay it only if you are late with your installments: it is not part of the expected cost.
Legal fees
On a mortgage you do pay them, but by rule they stay out of the APR: they are counted separately.
flow.after: What counts in the APR is whatever you are obliged to pay to get the loan. Left out are optional costs, those that arise from a delay on your part, and legal fees.

flow.q:
A €10,000 loan for one year, repaid all at the end.

• Interest (nominal rate 6%): €600
• Mandatory fees: €150, paid together with the repayment

What is the APR, as a percentage?
flow.exp:
Total cost: \(600 + 150 = \text{€}750\).

$$\text{APR} = \frac{750}{10{,}000} = 7.5\%$$

The nominal rate says 6%, but the loan costs 7.5%. If the fees were paid up front, the APR would rise a bit more, because in effect you would receive less than €10,000.

lessons.note: The nominal rate is the price of the money, the APR is the price of the whole loan. You compare the APR.

pairs: The pure interest rate of the loan
The annual cost of the loan, fees included
The sum you pay at each due date

ex.q: Loan A: nominal rate 5%, APR 8.2%. Loan B: nominal rate 6%, APR 6.9%. Same amount, same term. Which costs less?
ex.exp: What counts is the APR, which includes the fees: **B** costs 6.9% against 8.2% for A, even though it has the higher nominal rate.

lessons.title: The mortgage: fixed or adjustable

flow.q: To buy a home you take out a mortgage of €150,000, to be repaid over 25 years. If the rate goes from 3% to 5%, by how much does the monthly payment go up?
flow.after: At 3% the payment is **€711**, at 5% **€877**: about **€166 more every month**, for 25 years. On long terms even two points of rate weigh a lot.

flow.t: A long loan, with the house as collateral
flow.x:
The **mortgage** is the loan you take out to buy a home. The amount is large, so it is repaid over many years, usually between 15 and 30, with one payment each month.

To lend so much and for so long the bank wants a guarantee: the house itself. If you stop paying, it can have it sold and take its money back. This guarantee is called a **lien**.

Over such long periods interest weighs a lot. Look at how much you repay in all for €150,000 over 25 years:

[fig]

Same house, same amount: two more points of rate mean almost €50,000 more in interest.

When you sign a mortgage you choose how the rate will behave over the years.

With a **fixed rate** the rate stays what it was on day one, and so does the payment: you already know today how much you will pay in twenty years.

With an **adjustable rate** the rate follows a market benchmark rate, to which the bank adds a fixed markup, the **spread**. If market rates go up, your payment goes up; if they fall, it falls.

The adjustable often starts from a lower payment, but the risk that it rises is yours. The fixed often costs a bit more at the start: it is the price of certainty.

items: The payment stays the same to the end
It is the fixed rate that locks the payment for the whole term.
It follows a market rate plus the spread
That is exactly the definition of an adjustable rate.
If rates go up, the payment goes up
With a fixed rate the payment doesn't move: it only happens with the adjustable.
You already know today how much you will pay in 20 years
Only the fixed rate gives you this certainty.
If rates fall, you pay less
The adjustable follows the market even when it falls.

flow.x: A mortgage of €150,000. Move rate and term and see what happens to the payment and to total interest.

goals.label: Bring the payment to €800 or less
goals.hint: Lengthening the term isn't enough: try lowering the rate too.

goals.label: Now also keep total interest under €80,000
goals.hint: More years means more interest: try lowering the rate further or shortening the term.

flow.after: Lengthening the term lowers the payment, but raises total interest. To keep both low you need a lower rate: that is why it pays to compare several offers before signing.

lessons.note: Fixed: a certain payment. Adjustable: a payment that follows market rates. The choice depends on how much room you have if the payment goes up.

ex.q: You have an adjustable-rate mortgage and market rates go up. What happens to your payment?
ex.exp: An adjustable rate follows the market: if rates go up, your payment **goes up** too. With a fixed rate it would have stayed the same.

lessons.title: When debt works against you

flow.q: You paid for a sofa and a phone with a credit card: €2,000 of debt, at 18% a year. For 5 years you pay only the interest. How much have you paid in all at the end?
flow.after: Each year the interest is \(2{,}000 \times 18\% = \text{€}360\). In 5 years that makes **€1,800**, and you still owe all the original €2,000.

flow.t: The debt that doesn't go down
flow.x:
Some credit cards let you pay back what you spend a little at a time. They are called **revolving** cards. It looks convenient, but the rate is often very high, and the minimum payment they ask for covers almost only the interest.

With €2,000 of debt at 18% a year the interest is €360 a year, that is €30 a month. If you pay €30 a month, everything you pay goes to the bank as interest and the debt stays put.

[fig]

The debt only goes down with what you pay **on top of** the interest.
€2,000 of debt at 18% a year, that is 1.5% a month. Decide how much to pay each month.

goals.label: Pay off the debt within 2 years
goals.hint: With €30 you pay only the interest. Go up until the time drops to 2 years.

flow.after: With €30 a month you never finish. With €100 you pay it off in 2 years and pay about €396 in interest. The more you pay each month, the less the debt costs you.

flow.t: Which debt to pay off first
flow.x:
Money you use to reduce a debt stops costing you interest. It is like a safe investment that earns as much as the rate on the debt.

You have €1,000 free. See what happens in one year:

• in the savings account at 3% you earn €30;
• used to reduce the card at 18%, you save €180 of interest.

[fig]

That is why it usually pays to pay off the debts with the highest rate first.

fig.cap: In one year, with the same €1,000.

flow.t: You have some free money: in what order do you use it?
items: Emergency fund
Highest-rate debts
Investments
flow.after: It is a rule of thumb: first safety, then expensive debts, then the rest.

flow.q: You have a card debt at 18% a year and you reduce it by €500. How much interest do you save in a year?
flow.exp: \(500 \times 18\% =\) **€90** a year. In a savings account at 3% the same €500 would earn €15.

lessons.note: A debt at 18% costs more than almost any investment earns. Paying it off is the safest return you have.

ex.q: You have €1,000 free, a card debt at 18% and a savings account that earns 3%. What is the best thing to do?
options: Put it in the savings account
ex.exp: Paying down the debt saves you €180 of interest in a year, against the €30 you would earn in the savings account.

lessons.title: Buying in installments

flow.q: A €1,200 TV in 12 installments at zero interest. The contract has €30 of setup fees and €2 of fees on each installment. How much do you pay in all?
flow.after: The rate really is zero: you pay no interest. But you pay €30 for setup and \(2 \times 12 = \text{€}24\) on the installments: in all **€1,254**. Those extra €54, over a year, make an APR of 8.75%. Zero rate means a zero nominal rate, not zero cost.

flow.x:
**In an installment purchase, the price of the loan isn't only in the interest.**

The **nominal interest rate** measures interest. The **APR** puts interest and fees together: it is the only number that tells you how much the loan really costs in a year.

Fees are usually found in three places.

• **Setup fees**, paid once at the start.
• **Collection fees** on each installment and, in Italy, the stamp duty on the contract.
• **Insurance** sold together with the loan. If it is optional you can refuse it. If it is mandatory to get the loan, its cost has to be inside the APR.

A reference point for telling whether an offer is expensive: in Italy, the Bank of Italy's survey of spring 2026 puts the average APR of loans to buy goods at 11.3%, and of personal loans at 12.1%.

flow.t: Zero rate, but not zero APR
flow.x: A €1,200 purchase at zero interest. Move the fees and the number of installments.

goals.label: Bring the APR under 5%
goals.hint: The rate is already zero: the APR only drops by taking out fees.

goals.label: Now put back €30 of setup and €2 per installment, and go down to 6 installments
goals.hint: Put the fees back to the starting values, then shorten the plan.

flow.after: With the same fees, over 6 installments the APR rises to almost 13%. Fixed costs weigh more on small, short loans: that is why, on an installment purchase, even small fees matter.

flow.x:
In Italy, an installment purchase is a credit contract, and the law gives you four rights that few people use.

• **Change your mind.** You have 14 days to leave the financing without saying why.
• **Pay off early.** You can repay everything early whenever you want, and the costs of the loan are reduced for the time you don't use.
• **Stop the installments if the goods don't arrive.** If the seller doesn't deliver, or delivers something different, and doesn't put it right after your reminder, you can also have the financing linked to the purchase dissolved.
• **Know beforehand.** Before you sign they must give you a sheet with the APR, the installment and the total to repay, the same for all finance companies: it is there so you can compare two offers.

flow.t: What stays on record about you
flow.x:
In Italy, every time you apply for a loan, the application and the payments end up in **credit bureaus**, databases that finance companies check before they decide.

Both the good and the bad stay on record, for fixed periods:

| What | For how long |
|---|---|
| A loan application | 6 months |
| One or two late installments, then paid | 12 months |
| More than two late installments, then paid | 24 months |
| Installments never paid | 36 months |
| A loan repaid regularly | 60 months |

Two practical consequences. Even a small delay follows you for a year, and can cost you a mortgage. And applying for loans from many finance companies in the same month leaves a trace that doesn't help.

You can ask to see your data for free.

flow.t: Does it count in the APR?
items: The interest
It is the first item of the cost.
The setup fees
They are a compulsory cost of the loan.
The insurance the finance company requires
If they won't give you the loan without it, its cost counts in the APR.
The collection fees on each installment
You pay them with each installment: they are part of the cost.
The optional insurance you chose yourself
It isn't necessary to get the loan: it stays out of the APR. That is why it has to be looked at separately.
The late fee for an installment paid late
The APR is calculated as if you always paid on time.
flow.after: The APR counts everything you have to pay no matter what. What you add yourself, or what comes from a delay, stays out.

lessons.note: Zero rate means a zero nominal rate: the cost is in the fees, and the APR measures it. In Italy you have 14 days to change your mind, and delays stay on record for at least a year.

ex.q: A loan has a nominal rate of 0% and an APR of 9%. What does that mean?
options: That there is no interest, but there are fees
That there's an error in the contract
ex.exp: The nominal rate measures only interest, the APR fees too. With a zero nominal rate and an APR of 9% there is no interest, but there are fees: they are the cost of the loan.

ex.q: In Italy, you signed a financing agreement for a sofa yesterday and have changed your mind. What can you do?
options: Leave the contract: you have 14 days
Leave only by paying a penalty
ex.exp: On credit contracts you have 14 days to withdraw, without having to give any explanation.

ex.q: In Italy, you paid two installments late, then caught up. For how long does the record stay in the credit databases?
ex.exp: A delay of one or two installments, then paid, stays visible for 12 months from the moment you catch up. Beyond two installments the months become 24.

lessons.title: Buy now, pay later

flow.q: You pay for a €300 purchase in three interest-free installments, with a buy now, pay later service. Who pays for the cost of the service?
flow.after: The **store** pays it, with a fee on each sale. It is worth it to them, because people who can split a payment buy more often and spend more. That is the point to remember: the service is free for you because it works by getting you to buy.
options: Nobody: it is free for everyone

flow.x:
**Buy now, pay later is a small interest-free loan, granted in a few seconds at the checkout.**

Usually the price is split into three or four installments: the first right away, the others each month, taken automatically from your card.

If you pay on time it costs nothing. That is why it feels different from a debt, but it is a debt in every respect.

There are three risks, and none is written in large letters.

• **You buy more.** A €300 expense that becomes €100 feels smaller.
• **The installments add up.** Three purchases with three different services are three installment plans, and nobody shows you the monthly total.
• **Delay costs money.** If there is no money on the card when the installment comes due, late fees can apply, and the delay can be reported.

flow.q:
In October Elena makes three purchases with buy now, pay later, each in 3 equal installments:

• shoes for €240
• a jacket for €180
• headphones for €90

How much will be taken from her card in all in November?
flow.exp: Each purchase divided by three: \(80 + 60 + 30 =\) **€170**. The same again in December. They are small installments, but they arrive together and from three different services.

flow.t: In Italy, from November 20, 2026 it is credit in every respect

items: Three interest-free installments with a payments company
The deferral is granted not by the store but by a third company: it is credit.
The store lets you pay at the end of the month, at no cost
It is a free deferral from the seller, within 50 days.
Six installments over six months offered by the store, free
It goes beyond 50 days: the credit rules apply.
The store gives you 30 days, with a €3 fee
It has a cost: it is no longer a free deferral.
You pay the gym at the end of each month
You pay for a service after using it, with no extra cost.
flow.after: Only what is free, short and granted by the seller stays outside the rules.

lessons.note: Buy now, pay later is a debt without interest: free if you pay on time, but the installments add up. In Italy, from November 20, 2026, it follows the credit rules.

ex.q: Why should buy now, pay later be treated as a debt, even if it has no interest?
options: Because it always has hidden fees
Because it commits money you still have to earn
ex.exp: If you pay on time it costs nothing. But the installments of the coming months are money already promised: they add up with each other and with the rest of your fixed expenses.

ex.q: In Italy, from November 20, 2026, what must the company that grants you three installments on a purchase do?
options: Check beforehand that you can repay
Ask you for a guarantee on your home
ex.exp: Under the new rules it is consumer credit: whoever grants it must first assess whether you can repay, also considering your other debts.

ex.q: You miss an installment on a purchase paid in three parts. Besides the late fee, what do you risk?
options: That they take back the purchase
That the delay stays on record in the credit databases
ex.exp: Even a small debt, if paid late, can end up in the databases that banks check. You find it again when you ask for a loan or a mortgage.

lessons.title: The balance sheet

pages.x:
The **balance sheet** is a snapshot of a company on a specific day. It has two sides that always weigh the same.

• The **assets**: what the company owns, like cash, inventory and equipment.
• The **liabilities**: what it owes to others, like debts to banks and suppliers.
• The **equity**: what is left to the owners once all debts are paid.

$$\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Equity}$$

A company owns:

• cash 50
• inventory 150
• equipment 300

Total assets: **500**.

It owes 320 to banks and suppliers. Equity is what is left over:

\(500 - 320 =\) **180**

If the company earns and doesn't distribute profits, equity rises. If it loses, it falls.

lessons.note: \(\text{Assets} = \text{liabilities} + \text{equity}\). It is an equality that always holds, for every company.

ex.q: A company has assets of 800 and liabilities of 500. What is the equity worth?
ex.exp: \(800 - 500 =\) **300**. Adding the two figures is the typical mistake: equity is what is left over after the debts.

ex.q: A company ends the year with a loss and the owners put in no more money. What happens to equity?
ex.exp: The loss reduces what is left to the owners: equity **falls**. It rises when the company earns and keeps the profits in the company.

lessons.title: The income statement

pages.x:
The **income statement** tells the story of a period, usually a year: how much the company took in from sales, the **revenue**, and how much it spent, the **costs**. What is left is the **profit**.

You work down in steps:

• revenue minus the cost of goods sold = **gross margin**
• minus operating expenses, like salaries and rent = **operating income**
• minus interest and taxes = **net income**

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Revenue | 1,000 |
| Cost of goods sold | −600 |
| **Gross margin** | 400 |
| Operating expenses | −250 |
| **Operating income** | 150 |
| Interest | −30 |
| Taxes (30% of 120) | −36 |
| **Net income** | 84 |

The **net margin** is net income divided by revenue: \(\dfrac{84}{1{,}000} =\) **8.4%**. It tells how much of every €1 of sales stays with the company.

lessons.note: Revenue minus costs equals profit. Margins, as a percentage of revenue, let you compare companies of different sizes.

pairs: What the company owes to others
What is left to the owners

ex.q: A company has revenue of 2,000 and total costs of 1,700. What is the net margin?

lessons.title: Profit is not cash

pages.x:
The income statement records revenue and costs when they **arise**, not when the money moves. This rule is called the **accrual basis**.

• You sell goods for 100 with payment in 90 days: the revenue is there right away, the money isn't.
• You buy a machine for 1,000 that you will use for 5 years: you pay 1,000 right away, but the income statement counts 200 a year. That portion is called **depreciation**.

That is why a company can show a profit and still run out of cash.

The **cash flow statement** shows the real cash movements.

A company ends the year with a profit of 50. Assumption: all costs were paid in cash, but customers still owe 80 for sales already counted in revenue.

• Profit: +50
• Sales not yet collected: −80
• Change in cash: **−30**

The company earned, and yet it has 30 less in cash. Whoever evaluates a company always looks at both numbers.

lessons.note: Profit measures how much you earned, cash how much money you really have. They can go in opposite directions.

ex.q: A company has a profit of 120. All costs are paid, but customers still owe 200 for sales already counted. How did cash change?
ex.exp: \(120 - 200 =\) **−80**. The profit is there, but the money has not come in yet.

lessons.title: Price and value

pages.t: What you pay for €1 of profit
pages.x:
The price of a stock alone doesn't say whether it is expensive. A €30 stock can be more expensive than a €300 one.

A first yardstick is the **price/earnings** ratio, known as the **P/E**:

$$\text{P/E} = \frac{\text{stock price}}{\text{earnings per share}}$$

If the stock costs €30 and earnings per share are €2, the P/E is **15**: you pay €15 for every €1 of annual profit.

A high P/E usually means the market expects earnings to grow strongly. A low P/E can mean a bargain, or a company in trouble.

• Company A: price €30, earnings per share €2, P/E 15.
• Company B: price €60, earnings per share €2, P/E 30.

B costs double for the same earnings today. It makes sense only if its earnings will grow much faster. The P/E alone doesn't give the verdict: it helps you ask the right question.

lessons.note: The P/E tells how much you pay for each €1 of profit. It is used to compare similar companies, not as a final judgment.

ex.q: A stock costs €48 and earnings per share are €4. What is the P/E?
ex.exp: \(\dfrac{48}{4} =\) **12**: you pay €12 for every €1 of annual profit.

ex.q: Two companies in the same sector: A has a P/E of 10, B of 25. What does the comparison say?
options: For every €1 of profit, B costs more
ex.exp: The P/E says how much you pay for €1 of profit: €25 with B, €10 with A. It doesn't say who earns more, and a low P/E is not necessarily a bargain: it can signal a company in trouble.

lessons.title: Central banks and rates

pages.t: Who sets the price of money
pages.x:
A **central bank**, like the ECB for the euro or the Federal Reserve for the dollar, sets the **policy rates**: what banks pay to borrow money from the central bank and what they receive if they deposit it there. The rates on mortgages, loans and savings accounts depend on them, in a cascade.

The ECB's main task is to keep prices stable: its goal is inflation of 2% a year over the medium term.

• **Inflation too high**: the central bank **raises** rates. Borrowing money costs more, families and companies spend less, prices slow down.
• **Weak economy**: it **lowers** rates. Credit costs less, spending and investment pick up.

It matters a lot for investors: when rates rise, bonds already in circulation lose value and payments on adjustable-rate mortgages go up. When they fall, the opposite happens.

lessons.note: The central bank raises rates to curb inflation and lowers them to support the economy. Adjustable-rate mortgages and bonds are the first to feel it.

ex.q: Inflation is well above the target. What does the central bank usually do?
ex.exp: It raises rates: credit costs more, spending slows down and prices stop running.

ex.q: The central bank lowers rates. What effect does it usually have on new mortgages?
ex.exp: If money costs banks less, the rates banks charge customers usually fall too: new mortgages **cost less**.

us.title: Central banks and rates

pages.t: Who sets the price of money
pages.x:
A **central bank**, like the Federal Reserve (the Fed) in the US or the ECB in the euro area, sets the **policy rates**: the benchmark rates for what banks pay to borrow money. The rates on mortgages, loans and savings accounts depend on them, in a cascade.

The Fed has two tasks: stable prices and maximum employment. Its goal is inflation of 2% a year over the long run.

• **Inflation too high**: the central bank **raises** rates. Borrowing money costs more, families and companies spend less, prices slow down.
• **Weak economy**: it **lowers** rates. Credit costs less, spending and investment pick up.

It matters a lot for investors: when rates rise, bonds already in circulation lose value and payments on adjustable-rate mortgages go up. When they fall, the opposite happens.

us.note: The central bank raises rates to curb inflation and lowers them to support the economy. Adjustable-rate mortgages and bonds are the first to feel it.

ex.q: Inflation is well above the target. What does the central bank usually do?
ex.exp: It raises rates: credit costs more, spending slows down and prices stop running.

ex.q: The central bank lowers rates. What effect does it usually have on new mortgages?
ex.exp: If money costs banks less, the rates banks charge customers usually fall too: new mortgages **cost less**.

lessons.title: Exchange rates

pages.x:
The **exchange rate** is the price of one currency expressed in another. If the euro/dollar rate is 1.10, with €1 you buy $1.10.

• If the rate rises to 1.20 the euro has **strengthened**: with €1 you buy more dollars.
• If it falls to 1.00 the euro has **weakened**.

Whoever buys securities in another currency has two returns: that of the security and that of the exchange rate.

You buy American stocks for $1,100 when the rate is 1.10: you spend **€1,000**. Assumption: after a year the stocks are still worth $1,100, but the rate has risen to 1.20.

$$\frac{1{,}100}{1.20} = 916.67$$

In euros you have **€916.67**: you lost 8.3% without the stock moving. This is **currency risk**. It also works the other way: if the euro weakens, you gain.

lessons.note: With a security in a foreign currency you gain or lose because of the exchange rate too. Stronger euro: your dollars are worth less.

ex.q: You have $1,000. The euro/dollar rate goes from 1.00 to 1.25. How much are they worth now in euros?
ex.exp: \(\dfrac{1{,}000}{1.25} =\) **€800**. The euro has strengthened, so your dollars buy fewer euros.

ex.q: The euro/dollar rate goes from 1.10 to 1.00. What happened to the euro?
ex.exp: Before, with €1 you bought $1.10, now only $1.00: the euro **has weakened**.

us.title: Exchange rates

pages.x:
The **exchange rate** is the price of one currency expressed in another. If the euro/dollar rate is 1.10, one euro costs $1.10.

• If the rate rises to 1.20 the euro has **strengthened**: one euro now costs $1.20, so your dollars buy fewer euros.
• If it falls to 1.00 the euro has **weakened**: one euro costs only $1.00, so your dollars buy more euros.

Whoever buys securities in another currency has two returns: that of the security and that of the exchange rate.

You buy European stocks for €1,000 when the rate is 1.10: you spend **$1,100**. Assumption: after a year the stocks are still worth €1,000, but the rate has fallen to 1.00.

$$1{,}000 \times 1.00 = 1{,}000$$

In dollars you have **$1,000**: you lost 9.1% without the stock moving. This is **currency risk**. It also works the other way: if the euro strengthens, you gain.

us.note: With a security in a foreign currency you gain or lose because of the exchange rate too. Weaker euro: your euro stocks are worth less in dollars.

ex.q: You have €1,000. The euro/dollar rate goes from 1.00 to 1.25. How much are they worth now in dollars?
ex.exp: \(1{,}000 \times 1.25 =\) **$1,250**. The euro has strengthened, so each euro buys more dollars.

ex.q: The euro/dollar rate goes from 1.10 to 1.00. What happened to the euro?
ex.exp: Before, one euro cost $1.10, now only $1.00: the euro **has weakened**.

lessons.title: The business cycle
lessons.note: The economy alternates expansions and recessions. Two quarters of falling GDP are the rule of thumb for calling a recession.

ex.q: A country's GDP falls for two quarters in a row. What is this phase called?
ex.exp: Two consecutive quarters of falling GDP are the rule of thumb for calling a **recession**.

ex.q: In a recession, what do central banks usually do?
ex.exp: They lower rates, to make credit cheaper and get spending and investment going again.

lessons.title: Where your money goes

flow.q: On workdays Giulia has a coffee and a sandwich at the café: €6 a day, for about 220 days a year. How much does she spend in a year?
flow.after: €6 for 220 days: \(6 \times 220 =\) **€1,320**, almost a month of her salary, which is €1,600. It isn't a call to give up coffee. It is the reason it pays to know where your money goes: the small amounts that repeat are the ones you notice least.

flow.x:
**To decide where to send your money, you first need to know where it goes now.**

The money that comes to you in a month is called **income**: the salary you receive in your account, a pension, rent you collect.

The money that goes out is called **expenses**: everything you pay, from rent to coffee.

The difference between the two is the month's **balance**:

$$\text{balance} = \text{income} - \text{expenses}$$

Giulia earns €1,600 a month and spends €1,600: her balance is zero. She has no debts, but she isn't setting anything aside, and she couldn't say where it all went.

Expenses are not all the same. It helps to split them into two groups.

**Fixed expenses** come back every month for the same amount, or nearly, and you don't decide them each time: rent, bills, the phone plan, the car payment.

**Variable expenses** change from one month to the next and depend on what you do: grocery shopping, meals out, clothes, gas.

Here is Giulia's month:

[fig]

Fixed expenses rarely change, but when you manage it the saving repeats every month without effort. Variable ones can be changed right away, but you have to keep an eye on them every time.

items: Rent
It is the same amount every month and you don't decide it each time.
Dinner at a restaurant
It depends on how often you go out: it changes from one month to the next.
Phone plan
It renews every month for the same amount.
Clothes
You buy them when you decide, and the amount changes every time.
Car payment
It is set by the contract: the same every month.
Gas
It depends on how much you drive.
Gym membership
You pay it every month, whether you go or not.

flow.q:
Luca's month:

• salary: €1,900
• fixed expenses: €1,050
• variable expenses: €620

What is his balance for the month?
flow.exp: Expenses: \(1{,}050 + 620 = \text{€}1{,}670\). Balance: \(1{,}900 - 1{,}670 =\) **€230**. That is what Luca can set aside.

flow.x:
The balance is the first number to look at.

• If it is **positive**, something is left over: it is the basis of your **savings**.
• If it is **zero**, you get to the end of the month with nothing to spare, and one unexpected expense is enough to push you under.
• If it is **negative**, you are spending more than you earn: you pay the difference from earlier savings, or with debt.

To learn your real balance, one month of attention is enough: write down every expense, even small ones, then split them into fixed and variable.

Back to Giulia. Coffee and a sandwich cost her €1,320 a year, that is €110 a month. If she skipped the café on half the days, she would spend €55 less a month: her balance would go from zero to **+€55**, without changing salary.

lessons.note: \(\text{Balance} = \text{income} - \text{expenses}\). Fixed expenses come back the same every month, variable ones depend on what you do.

ex.q: In a month €2,000 comes in and €2,150 goes out. What happened?
options: You spent €150 more than you earned
ex.exp: \(2{,}000 - 2{,}150 =\) **−€150**. The balance is negative: you took that €150 from earlier savings, or from a debt.

ex.q: Which of these is a fixed expense?
ex.exp: The internet subscription comes back every month for the same amount: it is a **fixed expense**. Grocery shopping and gifts change each time: they are variable expenses.

lessons.title: A budget in three parts

flow.q: A simple rule says to split your salary into three parts: half for what you need, 30% for what you enjoy, 20% to set aside. On €1,600 a month, how much gets set aside each month?
flow.after: 20% of €1,600 is **€320** a month, or €3,840 in a year. Let's see how to build a plan like this, and what to do when the numbers don't add up.

flow.x:
**A budget is a plan: you decide in advance where the month's money will go, instead of finding out at the end.**

A simple way to do it is the **50/30/20** rule. Split your income into three parts:

• 50% for **needs**: what you can't do without, such as housing, bills, food, transport to work;
• 30% for **wants**: what makes life more enjoyable but could be cut back, such as eating out, trips, subscriptions;
• 20% for **savings**.

With Giulia's €1,600:

[fig]

It isn't a law. It's a starting point for checking whether your month is in balance.

items: Rent
You need a roof over your head: it is a need.
Electricity bill
A home can't do without it: it is a need.
Movie streaming subscription
It is nice to have, but it can be cut if necessary.
Groceries
Eating is a need. A restaurant, on the other hand, is a want.
Weekend at the beach
It is a pleasure: it can be postponed or scaled down.
Monthly train pass to get to work
You need it to earn your salary.
New phone, while the old one still works
As long as the old one works, replacing it is a choice.
flow.after: The line is not always sharp: groceries are a need, but wants end up in the cart too. What matters is being honest with yourself.

flow.t: When the numbers don't add up
flow.x:
In real life the three parts rarely come out right the first time. Giulia's actual month looks like this:

[fig]

Needs take €950 instead of €800, wants €600 instead of €480. That leaves €50 for savings.

She has two options, and she can use both:

• cut **wants**, which is the quickest way;
• cut **needs**, which is slower but lasts: a cheaper home, a cheaper electricity or phone plan.

There is also a trick that works: set the savings aside **as soon as your salary arrives**, with an automatic transfer, and live on what is left. That way your savings don't depend on how much is left over at the end of the month.

flow.t: Bring the month back into balance
flow.x: Giulia earns €1,600 a month. Move needs and wants and watch how much is left to set aside.

goals.label: Bring savings to at least €320 a month
goals.hint: The quickest way is to lower wants.

goals.label: Now reach €320 while leaving at least €450 for wants
goals.hint: If wants don't come down, needs have to: try lowering them.

flow.after: Cutting only wants works, but leaves little room to live. Lowering a fixed expense as well, such as rent or phone plans, frees up money every month without constant sacrifices.

flow.q: Marco earns €2,200 a month and wants to follow the 50/30/20 rule. What is the most he can put toward wants?

lessons.note: A budget decides in advance where the money goes. Starting rule: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings, set aside first.

ex.q: You earn €1,800 a month. With the 50/30/20 rule, how much do you set aside?
Why is it better to set your savings aside as soon as your salary arrives?
options: Because then they don't depend on how much is left at the end of the month
Because the bank pays more interest
ex.exp: If you wait until the end of the month you only save what is left over, and often nothing is. By setting it aside straight away, saving becomes the first expense of the month, not the last.

lessons.title: The emergency fund

flow.q: Paolo spends €1,400 a month and wants to set aside a reserve that covers 3 months of expenses, for emergencies. He saves €150 a month. How many months does he need to get there?
flow.after: He needs \(1{,}400 \times 3 = \text{€}4{,}200\). At €150 a month: \(\dfrac{4{,}200}{150} =\) **28 months**, more than two years. It sounds like a lot, but every month that passes Paolo is a little safer. That reserve has a name: emergency fund.

flow.x:
**The emergency fund is a sum kept aside only for the unexpected.**

Unexpected expenses aren't rare, they are just hard to predict: the furnace that breaks, the car at the mechanic, a trip to the dentist, a period without work.

Without a fund you have only two ways out. You can take out a loan, which costs interest. Or you can sell what you own in a hurry, maybe at the wrong moment.

With a fund the unexpected stays an annoyance, not a debt.

That is why the **emergency fund** comes before investments: it is what lets you leave them to work in peace.

The size is not the same amount for everyone: it depends on how much you spend.

The most widely used rule is to keep **3 to 6 months of expenses** aside. Expenses, not salary: what counts is how much you need to live.

Paolo spends €1,400 a month:

[fig]

When is the minimum enough, and when do you need more?

• Closer to **3 months** if you have a steady job and nobody depends on you.
• Closer to **6 months**, or even more, if your income is irregular, if you are self-employed or if you have a family to support.

flow.q: Chiara spends €1,650 a month and wants an emergency fund that covers 4 months. How much does she need to set aside?

flow.x:
The emergency fund has one job: to be there when you need it. It needs two qualities.

• It must be **liquid**: you must be able to use it within a few days, without penalties.
• It must be **stable**: it must not be able to drop in value just when you need it.

That is why it doesn't go into stocks, which can lose a lot in a few months, nor into a locked investment you can't touch.

It sits well in a checking account separate from your everyday one, or in a **savings account** you can withdraw from whenever you want.

It will earn little, and that is as it should be: it isn't there to make money, it is there to protect you. And after you have used it, the first thing to do is rebuild it.

flow.t: Is it an emergency fund expense?
items: Your car breaks down and you need it for work
It is sudden and can't be put off: it is exactly the case for the fund.
Summer vacation
You already know it is coming: you set a little aside each month.
Dental treatment that can't wait
It is urgent and it wasn't planned.
Christmas presents
Christmas comes every year on the same date: it isn't unexpected.
Two months without a salary
It is the most important case: the fund pays your expenses until your income returns.
The brand-new phone that just came out
It is a want: you buy it with the money for wants, not with the fund.
The car insurance, which renews every year
It is an expense you already know about: it goes in the budget.
flow.after: The fund is for what is urgent, necessary and unexpected all at once. Expenses you already know about go in the budget.

lessons.note: Emergency fund: 3 to 6 months of expenses, in a liquid and stable account. It comes before investments.

ex.q: Dario spends €1,200 a month, has a steady job and nobody depends on him. What is a reasonable size for his emergency fund?
ex.exp: With a steady job the minimum of the rule can be enough: 3 months of expenses, that is \(1{,}200 \times 3 =\) **€3,600**. A single month is too little. €36,000 is two and a half years of expenses: too much money sitting idle.

ex.q: Where does it make the most sense to keep the emergency fund?
options: In an investment locked for 5 years
In an account you can withdraw from right away
ex.exp: It has to be liquid and stable: an account you can withdraw from whenever you want. Stocks can fall just when you need the money, and a 5-year lock blocks it.

lessons.title: A goal, an amount, a date

flow.q: Elena wants to buy a used car in 2 years: she needs €6,000. She starts from zero and keeps the money in an account that earns nothing. How much does she need to set aside each month?
flow.after: €6,000 in 24 months: \(\dfrac{6{,}000}{24} =\) **€250** a month. A goal becomes a plan when it has an amount and a date.

flow.x:
**A vague goal stays a wish. With an amount and a date it becomes a plan.**

‘I'd like to put something aside for the car’ doesn't tell you what to do tomorrow. ‘I need €6,000 in 24 months’ does: a division is all it takes.

$$\text{monthly saving} = \frac{\text{amount}}{\text{months}}$$

For Elena: \(\dfrac{6{,}000}{24} =\) **€250** a month.

[fig]

If €250 a month is too much, there are only three levers: a lower amount, a later date, or a revised budget that frees up more money each month.

flow.t: Move the date or the amount
flow.x: Elena needs €6,000 for the car. Move how much she sets aside each month and for how many months.

goals.label: Reach the €6,000 she needs
goals.hint: You can raise the monthly saving, lengthen the duration, or both.

goals.label: Now get there setting aside at most €150 a month
goals.hint: With €150 a month you need more time: lengthen the duration.

flow.after: With €150 a month it takes 40 months instead of 24. The less you set aside each month, the further away the date moves: deciding which of the two matters more is up to you.

flow.q: You want to take a trip in 10 months and you need €1,800. How much do you need to set aside each month?

flow.x:
Not all goals are handled the same way. What counts is how much time is left.

• **Within 2 or 3 years**, like a car or a trip: the money has to stay safe, in an account. There is no time to recover from a drop.
• **Many years away**, like retirement: the money can be invested, because time works for you.

On long horizons part of the final amount isn't paid in by you: it is produced by returns, thanks to compound interest.

Here is €250 a month for 20 years, invested at 4% a year. Assumptions: constant return, payments at the end of each month.

[fig]

You paid in €60,000, but you end up with about €91,000. In reality the return changes every year, and it can be negative too: that is why you only invest money you won't need soon.

lessons.note: A goal has an amount and a date: amount divided by months gives the monthly saving. Near: keep the money safe. Distant: you can invest.

pairs: The money that comes to you in a month
The plan for how you will use your money
Money kept aside for the unexpected

ex.q: You need €3,000 in 15 months. How much do you need to set aside each month, not counting interest?
You have two goals: a car in 18 months and retirement in 30 years. Which money makes sense to invest in instruments that fluctuate?
ex.exp: With 30 years ahead there is time to recover from drops and to let compound interest work. The money for the car is needed in 18 months: it has to stay safe.

lessons.title: How insurance works

flow.q: A town has 1,000 families. Every year, on average, 2 houses suffer a fire that causes €100,000 of damage. If all the families split the cost of the damage, how much does each one pay in a year?
flow.after: The year's damage is \(2 \times 100{,}000 = \text{€}200{,}000\). Divided among 1,000 families, that is **€200** each. With €200 a year nobody risks losing €100,000: that is the idea behind every insurance policy.

flow.t: Many pay a little, a few receive a lot
flow.x:
**Insuring yourself means paying a small, certain amount so you don't risk a big, uncertain loss.**

A fire at home is rare, but if it happens to you it costs an amount you couldn't pay on your own. Nobody knows who it will hit. But we do know, quite precisely, how many there will be in all: out of 1,000 houses, about 2 a year.

An **insurance** company collects an amount from everyone every year, the **premium**, and with that money pays the damage of those who were hit. The sum that whoever suffered the damage receives is called the **payout**.

[fig]

The premium is higher than the simple division of the damage, because the company has to cover its costs and make a profit.

fig.cap: An example: real figures change from one policy to another.

flow.t: The contract is called a policy

flow.q: An insurance company covers 5,000 cars. Every year, on average, 100 of them have an accident that causes €3,000 of damage. How much should each car pay, just to cover the damage?
flow.exp: The year's damage: \(100 \times 3{,}000 = \text{€}300{,}000\). Divided among 5,000 cars: \(\dfrac{300{,}000}{5{,}000} =\) **€60**. The real premium will be higher, because it includes the company's costs and profit.

lessons.note: With insurance, many people pay a small, certain premium, and whoever suffers damage receives the payout. Always read what is excluded.

pairs: What you receive if you suffer the damage
The cases where the company doesn't pay

ex.q: You pay a €300 premium to insure your house and nothing happens during the year. What happens to the €300?
options: It counts as next year's premium
It stays with the company: you paid for a year of protection
ex.exp: The premium pays for the year's protection, whether you have damage or not. With the premiums of those who had no damage, the company pays those who did.

ex.q: Why is the premium higher than the average damage divided among the insured?
options: Because it includes the company's costs and profit
Because damage is always more than expected
ex.exp: Besides paying for damage, the company has offices, staff and a profit to earn. In the lesson's example: €200 of expected damage plus €60 of costs and profit.

lessons.title: Deductible and coverage limit

flow.q: Anna insured her house. The contract says she pays the first €500 of every damage. A pipe breaks and the water causes €3,000 of damage. How much does the insurance reimburse her?
flow.after: The first €500 stay with Anna: the insurer pays \(3{,}000 - 500 =\) **€2,500**. That part you pay yourself is called the deductible. Together with the coverage limit, which we will see shortly, it decides what a policy is really worth.

flow.x:
**Almost no policy pays the whole damage: part of it stays with you.**

The **deductible** is a fixed amount that stays with you for every damage. With a €500 deductible:

[fig]

What is it for? It removes small damages, which would cost the company more time than money. In exchange the premium goes down: the higher the deductible, the less the policy costs.

Sometimes, in place of the deductible, there is a **percentage deductible**: it works the same way, but it is a percentage of the damage instead of a fixed amount.

segs: Smaller than the deductible: you pay it all

flow.q: A policy with a €250 deductible. You have damage of €1,900. How much does the company reimburse you?

flow.x:
At the other extreme is the **coverage limit**: the highest amount the company pays, whatever the damage.

Anna's policy has a coverage limit of €50,000. If a fire caused €80,000 of damage, the company would stop at €50,000.

[fig]

That is why the coverage limit should be chosen by looking at the worst damage that can happen, not the most likely one. A policy with a low coverage limit costs less, but leaves you uncovered in exactly the case you insured against.

In short: small damages you pay yourself because of the deductible. Of enormous ones you pay the part above the coverage limit. In between, the company pays.

segs: The insurer pays, up to the coverage limit

flow.q: A policy with a €100,000 coverage limit and no deductible. The damage is €130,000. How much stays with you?
flow.exp: The company pays up to the coverage limit: €100,000. You are left with \(130{,}000 - 100{,}000 =\) **€30,000**.

items: A damage of €300
It is smaller than the deductible: it all stays with you.
The first €500 of a €4,000 damage
That is the deductible.
The other €3,500 of that damage
With the deductible removed, the company pays the rest.
The part above €50,000 of an enormous damage
Above the coverage limit the company doesn't pay.
A €20,000 damage, after the deductible
It falls between the deductible and the coverage limit: the company pays.

lessons.note: Deductible: the part of every damage you pay. Coverage limit: the ceiling above which the company doesn't pay. Together they tell you what a policy is worth.

ex.q: All else equal, what happens to the premium if you choose a higher deductible?
ex.exp: With a higher deductible you take on a bigger share of the damage. The company risks less and asks for a **lower** premium.

ex.q: You have a policy with a €1,000 deductible and suffer €800 of damage. How much do you receive?
ex.exp: The damage is smaller than the deductible: it all stays with you. The company starts paying only above €1,000.

lessons.title: What to really insure

flow.q: You have €400 a year to spend on insurance. Which of these risks makes the most sense to cover first?
flow.after: You insure first what would ruin you, not what would only annoy you. A broken screen is paid for with the emergency fund. Serious harm done to another person can cost more than you earn in many years.
options: Serious harm done to another person

flow.t: Big and rare, small and frequent
flow.x:
**The right question is not how likely it is, but: what happens to me if it happens?**

Every risk falls into one of these two boxes.

• **Small damages**, even if frequent: the broken phone, the washing machine to replace, a fine. They annoy you, but you can pay them with the budget or the emergency fund. Insuring them is rarely worth it: on average the premiums you pay exceed the payouts you receive, and you could have absorbed that damage yourself.
• **Big damages**, even if rare: the house destroyed, serious harm done to another person, an illness that keeps you from working for a long time. You can't pay them on your own. That is what insurance exists for.

[fig]

The emergency fund and insurance work together: the first covers small damages, the second those that the fund could never cover.

fig.cap: Example figures. The short bar is already longer than the true one: to scale it wouldn't be visible.

flow.x:
There is a risk many people forget: causing damage to someone else.

If because of you a person gets hurt or something breaks, the law obliges you to pay compensation. This obligation is called **liability**, and the insurance that covers it is liability insurance.
