For drivers it is so important that the law makes it mandatory almost everywhere: without **auto liability insurance** you can't drive. A serious accident can cost a six-figure sum, and without a policy you would have to pay it yourself.

It exists outside the car too. A liability policy for everyday life covers, for example, the flowerpot that falls from your balcony or the damage done while riding a bicycle. It usually costs little, because these cases are rare, but it covers very high amounts.

items: A fire in your home
It is an enormous damage, which you couldn't pay on your own.
The washing machine to replace
It costs a few hundred: that is the emergency fund's job.
Serious harm done to another person
It can cost very high amounts: you need liability insurance.
The broken phone screen
It is a small expense: you pay it with the money set aside.
An illness that keeps you from working for years
Losing income for a long time is one of the biggest risks.
A flat tire
It is a nuisance that costs very little.
Insurance required by law
The risks that would ruin you
Small damages, if you really want
flow.x: Tap the items from the most important to the least important.
flow.after: First what the law requires, then what you could never pay on your own. Small damages come last, and it is often better to leave them to the emergency fund.

lessons.note: You insure what would ruin you, not what annoys you. Small damages are covered by the emergency fund.

ex.q: Which risk makes the most sense to insure?
ex.exp: Insurance is for the losses you couldn't bear on your own. Small damages are paid with the emergency fund.

ex.q: Why is it usually not worth insuring a €150 item?
options: Because you can bear that loss yourself, and on average premiums exceed payouts
ex.exp: A €150 loss annoys you but doesn't put you in difficulty. And since the premium includes the company's costs and profit, on average you pay more than you receive.

lessons.title: Spotting a scam

flow.q: You are offered an investment that pays 10% a month, guaranteed. If it were true, how much would €1,000 become after 5 years?
flow.after: 10% a month for 60 months gives \(1{,}000 \times 1.10^{60}\), which is about **€304,000**. No real business grows like that, and if one existed it would not need your money. A return that high, and on top of that guaranteed, is the first sign of a scam.

flow.t: High and guaranteed don't go together
flow.x:
**Whoever promises you high, safe gains is hiding something from you.**

Return and risk go together. A savings account pays a few points a year precisely because the risk is low. To earn more you have to accept that things can go wrong.

That is why two words never go together: **high** and **guaranteed**.

[fig]

Whoever offers 10% a month is offering, in a single month, more than triple what a prudent investment returns in a whole year. If it were true, banks would be lining up to lend them money at much less.

rows.lab: A savings account, in one year

fig.cap: The 3% is an example: a savings account returns a few points a year.

flow.x:
The most common scam has a name: the **Ponzi scheme**. There is no investment at all. The gains paid to the first arrivals are the money paid in by the last.

Here is how it runs, with the promised 10% a month.

• 100 people pay in €1,000 each. There is €100,000 in the pot.
• Every month the scammer pays 10%, that is €10,000. The money comes out of the pot.
• The first ones are paid on time, they trust it and bring friends. The new money covers the payments.
• When new arrivals slow down, the pot empties. The payments stop and the principal is gone.

[fig]

Whoever gets in first sometimes really does earn, and that is what makes the scheme credible. But the money they collect is what was lost by those who came after.

rows.lab: Paid out as gains over 10 months
segs: The same money, returned in pieces

fig.cap: With no new arrivals the pot lasts 10 months. Then nothing is left.

flow.q: A scheme promises 5% a month. 200 people have joined, with €2,000 each. How much must the scammer pay each month to keep the promise?
flow.exp: There is \(200 \times 2{,}000 = \text{€}400{,}000\) in the pot. 5% of €400,000 is **€20,000** a month. No investment produces that: it comes out of the pot, that is, out of the money of those who paid in.

flow.x:
Scams change shape, but the signs are almost always the same.

• **High, guaranteed returns**: it is the clearest sign.
• **Hurry**: the offer expires today, spots are running out. It is there to stop you from thinking.
• **Lack of clarity**: it is not clear where the gains come from, and questions get vague answers.
• **Rewards for bringing friends**: the new money is used to pay the old.
• **No authorization**: to collect savings you need an authorization. In Italy the lists of who is authorized are public, on the websites of Consob and the Bank of Italy.

Before sending any money, do three things: check those lists, ask for everything in writing and take a few days. A serious offer will still be there in a week.

items: A guaranteed return of 5% a month
High and guaranteed together doesn't exist.
They tell you the value can also go down
It is what a serious operator has to tell you: every investment carries a risk.
The offer is only valid if you sign today
The hurry is there to stop you from thinking.
They hand you a document with costs and risks
Putting everything in writing is a sign of seriousness.
You earn more if you bring other investors
It is the mechanism that keeps a Ponzi scheme standing.
Whoever is offering is on the list of authorized operators
It is the first check to make, and here it went well.
They don't explain where the gains come from
If you don't understand how money is made, don't invest.

lessons.note: A high, guaranteed return doesn't exist. Distrust hurry, ask where the gains come from and check that whoever is offering is authorized.

ex.q: In a Ponzi scheme, where do the gains paid to the first investors come from?
options: From the money paid in by those who join later
From the profits of a real investment
ex.exp: There is no investment at all: the first ones' gains are the **money paid in by the last**. That is why the scheme holds up only as long as new people keep arriving.

ex.q: An acquaintance offers you a safe investment at 4% a month and asks you to decide by tonight. What do you do?
options: I pay in right away, before the spots run out
I pay in only a small amount, to try
I pay in nothing and check whether the person offering it is authorized
ex.exp: High return, guarantee and hurry are three warning signs together. Even a small amount risks being lost, and the first on-time payments are there precisely to get you to pay in more.

lessons.title: Phishing and identity theft

flow.q: A text message arrives in the same conversation where your bank sends you your codes: ‘Unusual account access. Verify now at this link.’ What do you think?
flow.after: The sender name of a text message and the number of whoever calls you can be faked: it is called **spoofing**. That is why a fake message can show up in the same conversation as the real ones. Since 2025 Italian carriers have blocked many calls from abroad that display a fake Italian number, but the trick has not gone away. The sender, on its own, never proves who is writing.
options: It is real: it is in the bank's conversation
It could be fake: the sender can be copied
Opening the link is enough to tell

flow.x:
**A scammer doesn't force the door: they talk you into opening it.**

• **Phishing**: an email that imitates the bank, the post office, a courier, a government agency.
• **Smishing**: the same message, by text or chat.
• **Vishing**: a phone call. It often comes right after the message: a fake operator, kind and well prepared, who guides you step by step.

The pattern is always the same: an urgent problem (the account blocked, the package held up, a refund on the way), a link to open or a number to call, and at the end a request for data or codes.

Three rules are almost always enough.

• The bank never asks for passwords, PINs or codes: not by email, not by text, not by phone.
• Don't go in through the link. Open the app yourself, or type the address yourself.
• If they call you, hang up and call back yourself, at the number on the card or on the website.

items: Text message: account suspended, log in from this link
Urgency plus a link: it is the classic pattern.
The app asks for your fingerprint for a payment you are making
It is strong authentication, and you started the payment.
An operator asks you for the code that arrived by text
Codes are for authorizing, never for blocking. No real operator asks for them.
Courier email: pay €1.99 to release the package
The small amount is there to get you to enter your card details.
App notification for a login you just made
It is a security alert, and it matches what you were doing.
They tell you to move your money to a safe account
The safe account is the scammer's. No bank asks for that.

flow.x:
**Scammers need more than your money: they need your data too.**

With a photo of an ID, the tax code (codice fiscale) and a fake pay stub, someone can apply for a loan in your name. They collect the money. The unpaid installments stay recorded under your name.

It is called **identity theft**. In Italy in 2025 more than 38,000 cases were uncovered, for over €165 million: on average €4,300 each.

You often find out late: from a reminder letter, or from financing that is refused to you for no reason.

How to reduce the risk:

• don't send photos of your documents to people you don't know, not even for a rental or sale listing;
• protect your email inbox with a password used nowhere else and with two-step verification: whoever gets in there can reset the passwords for everything else;
• every so often check what is recorded in your name at the credit bureaus: asking for it is free.

flow.t: Your data has been used: in what order do you move?
items: You block cards and access, from the app or the toll-free number
You change your passwords, starting with email
You file a report with the Polizia Postale, the Italian police unit for online crime
You send the report to the bank and the finance companies
flow.x: Tap the moves from the first to the last.
flow.after: First you stop the damage, then you document it. With the report in hand you dispute in writing the payments and loans you didn't ask for, and have the records in your name at the credit bureaus corrected.

lessons.note: The sender can be faked: never go in through a link and never give codes to anyone. Protect your documents and email. If your data is used: block, change your passwords, report, dispute.

ex.q: You get an email from your bank with a link to update your details. What is the safe way to check?
options: Open the link and see whether the site looks real
Open the bank's app yourself, without going through the link
Reply to the email and ask for confirmation
ex.exp: A fake site can be identical to the real one, and whoever sent the email is the one who answers it. The only safe check is to go in on your own, from the app or by typing the address.

ex.q: Why does the email inbox need more protection than any other service?
options: Because from there you can reset the passwords for almost everything
Because it is the hardest to get back into
ex.exp: Almost every service lets you reset your password with a link sent by email. Whoever controls your email can get into all the others, one at a time.

ex.q: A finance company sends you reminders for the installments of a loan you never applied for. What do you do?
options: You pay, to avoid being reported
You file a report and dispute the loan in writing
ex.exp: Paying would mean acknowledging a debt that isn't yours, and ignoring the letter lets the problem grow. With the report you dispute the loan and ask for the records in your name to be deleted.

lessons.title: Life insurance: protection or investment?

flow.q: Marco is 35, has two children and a mortgage. He wants his family to receive €200,000 if he dies in the next 20 years. How much does a policy that does only this cost each year?
flow.after: A **term life insurance** policy usually costs between €200 and €800 a year for amounts between €100,000 and €300,000, depending on age and health. It costs little because it pays only if the event happens, and at 35 that is rare. If at expiration Marco is alive he receives nothing: he bought protection, not an investment.

flow.t: Two products with the same name
flow.x:
**Two very different products are sold under the name life insurance: one protects, the other invests.**

• The **protection policy** is term life insurance. You pay a premium every year and, if you die within the chosen term, the people you named receive the death benefit. If at expiration you are alive, you receive nothing.
• The **investment policy**: you pay in money, the company invests it and later returns a lump sum to you. It can be a **with-profits policy**, linked to a prudent management by the company, or a **unit-linked policy**, linked to funds: there the value goes up and down, and the risk is yours.

Many policies mix the two. That is why, before signing, the question is one: do I need to protect someone, or to grow some money?

The question to ask is: **if my income disappeared tomorrow, who would be left in difficulty?**

• Young children, a partner who earns less, a mortgage to pay: protection is needed.
• Nobody depends on your income: as a rule it is not needed.

How big a death benefit? A simple way: the debt left on the mortgage, plus a few years of the family's expenses.

Four things to know.

• The premium depends on age, health and smoking: the younger you are, the less it costs.
• Answer the health questions precisely: a false answer can cause the payment to be refused.
• In Italy, premiums give a 19% tax credit, calculated on a maximum of €530 a year.
• In Italy, the sum paid to your loved ones is exempt from IRPEF and does not enter the estate: it goes to whoever you named.

flow.q: Giulia and Paolo have a mortgage with €120,000 of debt and spend €24,000 a year. They want to cover the mortgage plus three years of expenses. What amount do they insure?
flow.exp: Three years of expenses: \(24{,}000 \times 3 = \text{€}72{,}000\). Plus the mortgage: \(120{,}000 + 72{,}000 =\) **€192,000**.

flow.t: When the policy is an investment
flow.x:
An investment policy has real advantages: you choose who receives the money, without going through the estate, and as a rule those sums can't be seized.

It also has a price. Inside are the company's costs, the funds' costs and often a **premium charge**, that is, a percentage withheld on every payment. A Bank of Italy study measured that a unit-linked policy costs on average between 0.5 and 2.5 points a year more than buying the same funds directly.

It seems little. Over 20 years it is not:

[fig]

Two more things to check.

• **Leaving early costs**: in the first years what you get back can be less than what you paid in.
• The costs are written in the **KID**, the document of at most three pages that you must receive before signing.

fig.cap: An example with a fixed return of 4% a year, before taxes.

flow.t: Who needs a term life policy?
items: Father of two children, the only paycheck at home
If he is gone, the family is left with no income.
Single 25-year-old, no debts and no dependents
Nobody depends on their income.
Couple who have just taken out a thirty-year mortgage
The one who is left would have to pay the installment alone.
Retired woman with adult, independent children
The children have their own income: there is nobody to protect.
Single mother with a 6-year-old child
The child depends entirely on her.

lessons.note: Life insurance means two things: protection, which costs little and is needed if someone depends on your income, and investment, where you should check costs and exit penalties in the KID.

ex.q: You have a 20-year term life policy. At expiration you are alive. What do you receive?
options: Nothing: you paid for twenty years of protection
ex.exp: Term life insurance pays only if you die within the term. It is like home insurance: if nothing happens, the premium bought the protection of those years.

ex.q: In a unit-linked policy, who bears the risk that the funds go down?
ex.exp: In a unit-linked policy the amount follows the value of the funds. If they go down, what you get back goes down: the company doesn't guarantee the result, except what is written in the contract.

ex.q: Where do you find the costs of an investment policy, before signing?
options: Only in the statement, after the first year
ex.exp: The KID is the key information document: it shows the total costs and how much they weigh on the return, and it must be handed to you before signing.

lessons.title: All at once or a little at a time

flow.q: Davide invests €200 a month for 20 years in a fund that returns 5% a year on average. In all he pays in €48,000. How much does he end up with?
flow.after: With these assumptions he reaches about **€81,000**: €48,000 he paid in himself, the other €33,000 are returns. Assumptions: constant return of 5% a year, payments at the end of the month. In reality the return changes every year, but the idea holds: paying in a little for a long time works.

flow.x:
**You don't need a big sum to start investing: you can begin small, every month.**

There are two ways to put money into an investment.

• A **lump sum**: you put in a sum all at once. It is the case of someone who already has money set aside, for example an inheritance.
• **Dollar-cost averaging**: you put in a fixed amount at regular intervals, usually every month. It is the case of someone who invests part of their paycheck.

[fig]

Dollar-cost averaging has a practical advantage: it becomes a habit. Once the automatic payment is set up, you invest without having to think about it and without having to decide each time whether it is the right moment.

rows.lab: Lump sum: all on day one

flow.x:
Back to Davide: €200 a month for 20 years, at 5% a year.

[fig]

Every payment starts earning from the day it goes in, and the returns produce more returns: it is compound interest. The first €200 work for almost twenty years, the last ones haven't yet had time to earn.

That is why starting early matters so much.

| Duration | Paid in | At the end |
|---|---|---|
| 10 years | €24,000 | €30,873 |
| 20 years | €48,000 | €81,161 |
| 30 years | €72,000 | €163,075 |

From 10 to 20 years the amount paid in doubles, but the final amount does much more. From 20 to 30 years you add €24,000 of payments and find about €82,000 more.
Every month you pay in an amount and invest it at 5% a year. Move the levers and see how much you will have at the end.

goals.label: Reach at least €100,000
goals.hint: Try lengthening the duration, or raising the payment.

goals.label: Now get there paying in less than €50,000 in all
goals.hint: Less money paid in means more work left to time: lengthen the duration and lower the payment.

flow.after: You can reach €100,000 paying in less than half of it, but only by giving the plan many years. Whoever starts late has to pay in much more to reach the same amount.

flow.q: You invest €150 a month with dollar-cost averaging. How much have you paid in, in all, after 8 years?
flow.exp: \(150 \times 12 = \text{€}1{,}800\) a year. In 8 years: \(1{,}800 \times 8 =\) **€14,400**. The value of your investment will be different, because it depends on returns.

lessons.note: Lump sum: all at once. Dollar-cost averaging: a fixed amount every month. With dollar-cost averaging, time matters most: the sooner you start, the more compound interest works.

ex.q: What sets dollar-cost averaging apart from investing a lump sum?
options: With dollar-cost averaging you pay in a fixed amount at regular intervals, with a lump sum everything at once
Dollar-cost averaging is guaranteed, a lump sum is not
Dollar-cost averaging can only be done with bonds
ex.exp: Dollar-cost averaging means regular payments, a lump sum means a single payment. Neither is guaranteed: both invest in instruments that can rise and fall.

ex.q: Anna and Bruno each pay €200 a month into the same fund. Anna starts at 25, Bruno at 35. Both stop at 65. Who will have more?
options: Bruno, because he started with more experience
Anna, because her money worked 10 years longer
They will have the same amount
ex.exp: Anna pays in for 40 years, Bruno for 30. Anna has paid in €24,000 more, but above all her first payments had ten more years to produce returns on returns.

lessons.title: Buying at different prices

flow.q: You invest €100 a month in a fund. The price of one share is €10 the first month, €8 the second, €12.50 the third. In which month did you buy the most shares?
flow.after: With a fixed amount you buy more shares when the price is low: \(\dfrac{100}{8} =\) **12.5 shares** in the second month, against 10 in the first and 8 in the third. It is a small automatic advantage of always paying in the same amount.

flow.x:
**With dollar-cost averaging you don't always buy the same quantity: you always buy for the same amount.**

A fund is divided into **shares**, and the price of a share changes over time. If you pay in €100 a month, how many shares you receive depends on that day's price:

$$\text{shares} = \frac{\text{amount paid in}}{\text{price of one share}}$$

[fig]

When the price falls your €100 buys more, when it rises it buys less. Without deciding anything, you end up buying more shares at low prices than at high prices.

flow.q: In three months you have paid in €300 and bought 10 shares, then 12.5, then 8. How many shares do you have in all?

flow.x:
How much did each share cost you, on average? It is called the **average purchase price**:

$$\text{average price} = \frac{\text{total paid in}}{\text{shares owned}}$$

You paid in €300 and you have 30.5 shares: \(\dfrac{300}{30.5} =\) **€9.84** a share.

The average of the three prices, instead, is \(\dfrac{10 + 8 + 12.50}{3} =\) **€10.17**.

Your cost is lower than the average of the prices, precisely because you bought more shares when they cost less.

Be careful not to ask dollar-cost averaging for what it can't give. It doesn't protect you from losses: if the price falls below €9.84 you are at a loss. And if prices always rise, whoever paid in everything up front did better. Its strength is something else: it saves you from having to guess the right moment to get in.

flow.q: With dollar-cost averaging you have paid in €1,200 in all and own 100 shares. Today one share is worth €13. How much is your investment worth?
flow.exp: 100 shares at €13 each: \(100 \times 13 =\) **€1,300**. Your average purchase price is \(\dfrac{1{,}200}{100} = \text{€}12\): today the share is worth more, so you are earning €100.

flow.t: True or false about dollar-cost averaging?
items: With the same amount you buy more shares when the price is low
It is a division: a fixed amount divided by a lower price gives more shares.
Dollar-cost averaging guarantees you will not lose
If the price falls below your average purchase price, you are at a loss.
It saves you from choosing the right moment to get in
You get in a little at a time, at different prices.
If prices always rise, dollar-cost averaging beats a lump sum
In that case whoever paid in everything up front bought at the lowest prices.
The average purchase price is the total paid in divided by the shares
That is exactly the definition.

lessons.note: With a fixed amount you buy more shares when they cost less. The average purchase price is the total paid in divided by the shares: it is your breakeven point.

ex.q: You pay in €200 when a share costs €20 and another €200 when it costs €10. What is your average purchase price?
ex.exp: Shares bought: \(\dfrac{200}{20} = 10\) and \(\dfrac{200}{10} = 20\), 30 in all. Average purchase price: \(\dfrac{400}{30} =\) **€13.33**. It is not €15, the average of the two prices, because at €10 you bought twice as many shares.

ex.q: Your average purchase price is €9.84 and today a share is worth €9. How is your investment doing?
ex.exp: Each share cost you €9.84 on average and today it is worth €9: you are **at a loss**. The average purchase price is your breakeven point.

lessons.title: The rule of 72

flow.q: You invest €5,000 and let it grow at 6% a year, without touching it. After how many years will it have become €10,000?
flow.after: It takes about **12 years**. There is a shortcut to know it without a calculator: divide 72 by the rate. \(\dfrac{72}{6} = 12\).

flow.t: A division instead of a formula
flow.x:
**To know in how many years your money doubles, just divide 72 by the rate.**

$$\text{years to double} \approx \frac{72}{\text{rate}}$$

The rate is written as a number: for 6% you put 6. It works thanks to compound interest: every year the interest is added to the principal and the next year it earns interest too.

| Rate | Rule of 72 | Exact calculation |
|---|---|---|
| 2% | 36 years | 35.0 years |
| 4% | 18 years | 17.7 years |
| 6% | 12 years | 11.9 years |
| 8% | 9 years | 9.0 years |

It is an estimate, not a precise calculation, but for the rates you usually meet it is off by only a few months.

Notice one thing: going from 2% to 4% doesn't shorten the wait a little. It halves it.

flow.q: An investment returns 3% a year. According to the rule of 72, in how many years does it double?

flow.t: It works for everything that grows
flow.x:
The same rule works for anything that grows at a constant pace. Prices too.

With inflation of 3% a year, prices double in about \(\dfrac{72}{3} =\) **24 years**. It means that money left idle, in 24 years, buys half as much.

[fig]

And it works for debts. A debt at 18% a year on which you pay nothing doubles in about \(\dfrac{72}{18} =\) **4 years**.

The rule of 72 is for this: to feel how much a rate weighs without doing the math. 2% and 6% look close. But one doubles your money in 36 years, the other in 12.

flow.q: With inflation of 4% a year, in about how many years do prices double?
flow.exp: \(\dfrac{72}{4} =\) **18 years**. In 18 years money left idle buys about half as much.

flow.t: From the fastest doubling to the slowest
items: Credit card debt at 18%
Investment at 8%
Investment at 4%
Savings account at 2%
flow.x: Tap the items from the one that doubles first to the one that doubles last.
flow.after: 72 divided by the rate: about 4 years, 9 years, 18 years, 36 years.

lessons.note: \(\text{Years to double} \approx \dfrac{72}{\text{rate}}\). It works for invested money, for prices and for debts.

ex.q: At about what annual rate does money double in 10 years?
ex.exp: The rule also works in reverse: \(\text{rate} \approx \dfrac{72}{\text{years}} = \dfrac{72}{10} =\) **7.2%**.

ex.q: You have €2,000 invested at 8% a year. According to the rule of 72, about how much will you have after 18 years?
ex.exp: At 8% money doubles every \(\dfrac{72}{8} = 9\) years. In 18 years it doubles twice: from €2,000 to €4,000, then to **€8,000**.

lessons.title: Splitting and rebalancing

flow.q: Marta invests €10,000: €6,000 in stocks and €4,000 in bonds. In a year the stocks rise 30%, the bonds stay flat. What percentage of her portfolio is now in stocks?
flow.after: The stocks are worth \(6{,}000 \times 1.30 = \text{€}7{,}800\), the bonds €4,000. In all €11,800, and the stocks are \(\dfrac{7{,}800}{11{,}800}\), that is about **66%**. Marta did nothing, yet her portfolio became riskier than the one she had chosen.

flow.x:
**Before choosing which securities to buy, you decide how to split your money between stocks and bonds.**

The whole of your investments is called a portfolio. The way you split it has a name: **asset allocation**. It is the choice that weighs most on how much it can rise and fall.

• More **stocks**: more expected growth over the long run, but bigger drops along the way.
• More **bonds**: less expected growth, but a calmer ride.

[fig]

There is no split that is right for everyone. It depends on how much time you have before you need the money, and on how much you can bear to watch it fall without selling.

Marta has 15 years ahead and chooses 60% stocks and 40% bonds.

fig.cap: Three examples. The names change from one provider to another.

flow.x:
Once chosen, the split doesn't stay put: the markets move it.

After a year in which stocks rise 30% and bonds stay flat, Marta's portfolio has changed:

[fig]

Stocks went from 60% to 66%. If they kept rising they would reach 70%, then 80%. Marta would find herself with a portfolio much riskier than the one she chose, right after a long climb: that is, when a drop would hurt most.

flow.t: Bringing it back to where you decided
flow.x:
To **rebalance** means to bring the portfolio back to the split you chose.

Marta wants to go back to 60% stocks on €11,800:

• stocks she should have: \(11{,}800 \times 60\% =\) **€7,080**
• stocks she has: €7,800
• to sell: \(7{,}800 - 7{,}080 =\) **€720**

With those €720 she buys bonds, which rise to €4,720: 40%.

She sold a bit of what went up and bought what stayed behind. It is the opposite of what instinct would say, and that is why it is best done with a fixed rule, for example once a year.

Rebalancing is not for earning more: it is for keeping the risk where you decided. Selling can trigger taxes and fees, so it shouldn't be done too often.

flow.q: A portfolio is worth €20,000: €14,000 in stocks and €6,000 in bonds. You want to go back to half and half. How much of the stocks do you need to sell?
flow.exp: Half of €20,000 is €10,000. You have €14,000 in stocks: you sell \(14{,}000 - 10{,}000 =\) **€4,000** and with that money you buy bonds, which rise to €10,000.

items: You need the money in 25 years
With so much time ahead you can bear the drops and aim for growth.
You need the money in 3 years
With little time a big drop can't be recovered: you need a calmer ride.
A 20% drop would keep you awake at night
If you would end up selling at the worst moment, better a portfolio that swings less.
You have just started working and are investing for retirement
It is the typical case of a very long horizon.
You retire next year
Soon you will need that money to live on.

lessons.note: Asset allocation is how you split your money between stocks and bonds. The markets move it: rebalancing brings it back to where you decided.

ex.q: You chose 50% stocks and 50% bonds. After a year the stocks have risen a lot and are now 60%. What does rebalancing mean?
options: Buying more stocks, since they are rising
Selling some of the stocks and buying bonds
ex.exp: Rebalancing brings the portfolio back to the chosen split: you **sell part of what went up** and buy what stayed behind, until you are back to 50 and 50.

ex.q: What is rebalancing mainly for?
options: To keep the risk at the level you chose
ex.exp: It is for not finding yourself, after a long climb, with many more stocks than you had decided on. It doesn't promise higher returns, and selling can in fact trigger taxes.

lessons.title: Losses hurt more

flow.q: A game: you flip a coin. If it comes up heads you win €150, if it comes up tails you lose €100. If you could repeat it many times, how much would you earn on average on each flip?
flow.after: Half the time you win €150, half the time you lose €100: on average \(0.5 \times 150 - 0.5 \times 100 =\) **+€25** per flip. It is a game worth playing. And yet, faced with a single flip, many people refuse: the fear of losing €100 weighs more than the hope of winning €150.

flow.x:
**Losing €100 hurts more than gaining €100 feels good.**

Researchers call it **loss aversion**. In experiments, to accept the risk of losing €100 people ask on average to be able to win about €200. A loss weighs roughly double a gain of the same size.

[fig]

It is not a flaw to be fixed: it is how we are built. But when investing it leads to wrong decisions, because markets rise and fall all the time, and every drop is felt twice as much as every rise.

fig.cap: A rough measure: it varies from person to person.

flow.x:
Loss aversion pushes toward three typical mistakes.

• **Holding losing investments too long.** As long as you don't sell, the loss seems not to exist. So you wait to break even, even when the reasons you bought are gone.
• **Selling winning investments too early**, out of fear of watching that gain disappear.
• **Looking too often.** Whoever checks every day sees many more negative days than whoever looks once a year, and every negative day hurts.

One idea helps against all three: the market doesn't care what price you bought at. The useful question isn't ‘how much am I losing?’ but ‘if I had this money in hand today, would I buy this investment?’ If the answer is no, the purchase price is not a reason to hold on to it.

flow.q: Another coin game: heads you win €300, tails you lose €200. How much do you earn on average on each flip?
flow.exp: \(0.5 \times 300 - 0.5 \times 200 = 150 - 100 =\) **+€50** per flip. It is a favorable game, even if the possible loss of €200 is scary.

flow.t: Is it an effect of loss aversion?
items: I won't sell until I break even
The purchase price becomes a finish line, but the market doesn't care.
I immediately sell a stock that has risen 5%, afraid it will fall
The fear of losing a gain makes people sell too early.
I check my portfolio ten times a day
The more you look, the more negative days you see, and each one weighs double.
I sell because I have reached the amount I needed
It is a decision tied to your goal, not to fear.
I rebalance once a year, as per the plan
It is a rule decided beforehand, with a cool head.

lessons.note: A loss hurts about twice as much as an equal gain feels good. Decide by looking ahead, not at the price you bought at.

ex.q: You bought a stock at €50 and it is now worth €30. In the meantime the company has lost its best customers. What is the healthiest way to think about it?
options: I ask myself whether I would buy it today at €30
I wait for it to go back to €50, then sell
I buy more to lower my average price
ex.exp: The €50 you paid no longer counts: what counts is what the stock is worth today and what you expect for the future. If you wouldn't buy it today, the purchase price is not a reason to keep it.

ex.q: What does loss aversion say?
options: That a loss weighs more than a gain of the same size
That losses recover on their own
ex.exp: Losing €100 hurts about twice as much as gaining €100 feels good. It says nothing about how your investments will do: it says how you will react.

lessons.title: Everyone is buying, so I buy too

flow.q: A stock goes from €10 to €40 in a year. Everyone is talking about it, and Luca buys at €40. Then the price goes back to €16. How much did Luca lose, in percentage?
flow.after: Luca bought at €40 and ends up with €16: he lost €24 out of €40, that is **60%**. Whoever bought at €10 is still up 60%. Same stock, same story: what made the difference was the moment of entry.

flow.x:
**When a price rises and everyone is talking about it, you feel like buying. It is often the worst moment to do it.**

Watching others earn while you stand by and watch creates a very strong push. It has a name by now in common use: **FOMO**, fear of missing out.

Another habit works alongside it: **herd behavior**. If everybody is doing it, we think, there must be a reason. In everyday life that is often a good rule. In markets it isn't, for a simple reason: the more people have already bought, the more the price has already risen.

[fig]

When a piece of news has reached you, it is likely already in the price.

rows.lab: When everyone is talking about it

flow.x:
When herd behavior takes over a whole market, a **bubble** forms: prices rise far more than what you are buying is really worth.

It usually goes like this.

• Something new catches attention, and the first prices rise for good reasons.
• The first buyers' gains attract more buyers. The price rises because people buy, and people buy because the price rises.
• Then come those who buy only to resell at a higher price. Nobody looks at what they are buying anymore.
• The new buyers run out. The price stops rising, someone sells, and the fall is faster than the rise.

It happened with tulips in the Netherlands in the seventeenth century, with internet stocks in the late nineties, with houses in the United States before 2008. The object changes, the script doesn't.

flow.t: Put the phases of a bubble in order
items: Something new attracts the first buyers
Prices rise and everyone else arrives
People buy only to resell for more
The buyers run out and the price collapses
flow.after: Whoever enters in the third phase buys from whoever entered in the first.

flow.q: You buy a stock at €80, at the height of the enthusiasm. The price falls to €20. By what percentage must it rise to get back to €80?
flow.exp: From €20 to €80 is €60 more: \(\dfrac{60}{20} =\) **300%**. The price has to quadruple. After a 75% drop, a +75% is not enough.

flow.x:
You don't need to be able to predict bubbles. You need not to get carried away.

• **Decide beforehand.** A written plan, with how much you invest each month and in what, takes the decision away from you at the moment when you are most emotional.
• **Ask yourself the uncomfortable question.** Am I buying because I understood what I'm buying and what it is worth, or because it went up?
• **Look at how much it weighs.** A small part of your money on a risky idea is a choice. All of your savings is not.

Whoever invests a fixed amount every month in a well-diversified fund already has a good defense: they always buy, both when everyone is enthusiastic and when everyone is afraid.

lessons.note: When everyone is buying, the price has already risen. Decide with a plan written beforehand, not with the fear of missing out.

ex.q: A stock has tripled in six months and everyone is talking about it. What does this say about its future?
options: Nothing certain: it only says that today it costs much more
ex.exp: A past rise promises neither more rise nor a collapse. It only says that whoever buys today pays three times as much, so has less margin if things go wrong.

ex.q: What sets a bubble apart from a normal rise in prices?
options: In a bubble people buy mainly because the price is rising
In a bubble prices rise slowly
In a bubble only professionals buy
ex.exp: In a bubble the price rises because people buy, and people buy because the price rises. Nobody looks anymore at how much what they are buying is really worth.

lessons.title: Selling at the worst moment

flow.q: Sara has €10,000 invested. The market loses 30% and she, gripped by fear, sells everything. The next year the market rebounds 50%, but Sara stayed out. How much less money does she have compared with someone who didn't sell?
flow.after: Whoever stayed invested has \(10{,}000 \times 0.70 \times 1.50 = \text{€}10{,}500\). Sara sold at €7,000 and stayed there: she has **€3,500** less. The 30% loss was only on paper. By selling she made it final.

flow.x:
**As long as you don't sell, a drop is a number on a screen. It becomes a real loss the moment you sell.**

When markets fall hard, the news talks about a crash and every day the number is lower. The natural reaction is to run: sell everything so as not to lose more.

The problem is that sharp drops and sharp rebounds are often close together. Whoever gets out after the drop shelters from a fall that has already happened, and misses the rebound that comes after.

[fig]

To do better than someone who stays put you have to get two moments right: when to get out and when to get back in. Getting just one wrong is enough to do worse.

Falling is part of how stock markets work. In the history of the big stock markets, drops of 10% have come on average every year or two, and those of 30% or more about once every ten years.

So far the big markets have always recovered: sometimes in a few months, sometimes after many years. It is not a guarantee for the future. But for someone with a lot of time ahead, a drop is a stretch of road, not the end of the journey.

Three things make it easier to stay put.

• **Invest only money you don't need soon.** Whoever needs it in a year is forced to sell, at any price.
• **Have an emergency fund.** That way an unexpected expense doesn't force you to sell at the wrong moment.
• **Choose a split you can bear.** If a −30% would keep you awake at night, you need fewer stocks.

flow.q: You have €8,000 invested. The market falls 25% and then rebounds 40%. If you don't sell, how much do you have at the end?
flow.exp: After the drop: \(8{,}000 \times 0.75 = \text{€}6{,}000\). After the rebound: \(6{,}000 \times 1.40 =\) **€8,400**. A −25% followed by a +40% doesn't make +15%: percentages multiply, they don't add.

flow.t: Does it help you not sell in a panic?
items: Having an emergency fund
An unexpected expense doesn't force you to sell.
Checking prices every hour
The more you look, the scarier the drop feels.
Having invested money you need in 20 years
With so much time, a drop can be waited out.
Having put everything in a single stock
A single stock may never recover: diversifying is for this too.
Having a plan written beforehand
The decision has already been made, with a cool head.
Listening to those shouting about a crash
Other people's fear is contagious.

lessons.note: A drop becomes a real loss only when you sell. Time, an emergency fund and a written plan help you stay put.

ex.q: Your diversified fund has lost 20% and you will need that money in 25 years. What does someone with a plan usually do?
options: Sells everything and waits for better times
Moves everything into a single stock that is rising
ex.exp: With 25 years ahead, a 20% drop is a stretch of road. Whoever keeps paying in buys at lower prices during that period.

ex.q: Why is it so hard to profit by getting out of the market and back in?
options: Because you have to get two moments right: when to get out and when to get back in
ex.exp: You have to nail both the moment to get out and the moment to get back in. Whoever gets out after a drop often gets back in when prices have already recovered.

lessons.title: Feeling smarter than the market

flow.q: Luca has €10,000 invested and buys and sells often: 40 trades a year, and each one costs him an €8 fee. How much does he spend in fees in 10 years?
flow.after: \(40 \times 8 = \text{€}320\) a year, that is **€3,200** in ten years: almost a third of the starting €10,000, spent just to move around. To break even, every year Luca has to do 3.2% better than someone who stays put.

flow.x:
**Almost all of us think we are better than average. By definition, it can't be true for everyone.**

It is called **overconfidence**. Ask a group of people whether they drive better than average: the great majority say yes.

In investing the same happens, with an aggravating factor: chance disguises itself as skill. If you buy a stock and it rises, you think you understood it. If it falls, it was bad luck. After a few lucky hits you feel like an expert and start taking more risk.

On the other side of every purchase of yours, though, there is someone selling. Often it is a professional who does this job all day, with more information and more tools than you. It is not impossible to do better than them. It is just much less likely than it seems.

Overconfidence has an effect that can be measured: it makes people buy and sell too much.

Every trade has a cost. There is the **fee** you pay the broker. And there are taxes on gains, which you pay every time you sell at a gain instead of putting them off.

Here are Luca's €10,000 and his ten years of fees:

[fig]

Studies on small investors have found the same result for years: on average, whoever trades more earns less. Not because they pick worse stocks, but because costs eat the results.

Often the move that pays the most is doing nothing.

flow.q: You make 25 trades a year and each one costs a €6 fee. You have €5,000 invested. How much do the fees weigh in a year, as a percentage of the capital?
flow.exp: \(25 \times 6 = \text{€}150\) a year. \(\dfrac{150}{5{,}000} =\) **3%**. Before you even earn anything, you have to make up the 3%.

flow.t: The rules of someone who doesn't trust themselves
flow.x:
Good investors are not the ones who don't have these weaknesses. They are the ones who know they have them and give themselves rules.

• **Write the plan beforehand**: how much you invest, in what, for how long.
• **Make it automatic**: a fixed payment every month decides in your place.
• **Diversify**: that way you don't have to be right about a single stock.
• **Look rarely**: once or twice a year is enough to rebalance.
• **Keep costs low**: costs are the only certain thing about an investment.

They are the ideas of this whole course, lined up. None of them requires predicting the future, and that is why they work.

lessons.note: Feeling better than average makes you trade too much, and trading costs money. A written, automatic, low-cost plan almost always beats instinct.

pairs: A loss weighs more than an equal gain
Doing something because everyone is doing it
The fear of being left out of a gain
Believing you are better than average

ex.q: You have picked three stocks in a row correctly. What does it prove?
options: That you can predict the market
Little: three hits can be luck
That you should bet everything on the next one
ex.exp: Three results are too few to tell skill from luck. The risk is feeling like an expert and starting to bet bigger amounts.

ex.q: Two investors have the same portfolio. One makes 50 trades a year, the other 2. With the same return before costs, who ends up with more?
ex.exp: Every trade costs a fee, and often taxes too. With the same return before costs, whoever trades less keeps more.

lessons.title: Renting or buying

flow.q: You buy a house for €200,000 and after three years you have to move to another city. You sell it at the same price. Compared with renting at €800 a month, how did it go?
flow.after: In three years rent would have cost €28,800. By buying you paid about €16,000 in purchase costs, €16,000 in interest, maintenance, and you kept your savings tied up: in all about €41,600. Rent is not money thrown away: it is the price of a service. Whoever buys also has money that doesn't come back, it just shows less.
options: Better: rent is money thrown away

flow.t: The money that doesn't come back
flow.x:
**Whoever rents pays rent. Whoever buys pays four other things, and none of them is returned.**

• The **purchase costs**: taxes, legal fees, agent. They are paid once and are not recovered when you sell.
• The mortgage **interest**. The part of each payment that repays principal is saving, the interest is not.
• **Maintenance** and extraordinary expenses, which with a rental fall on the owner.
• The **return you give up** on the down payment: that money, invested, would have earned something.

In exchange the buyer has two advantages: no rent to pay, and if the house rises in value the gain is theirs. If it falls, so is the loss.

That is why the right question isn't whether buying pays off, but **after how many years**. Purchase costs all weigh at the start: the longer you stay in the house, the more they are spread out.

flow.t: After how many years it pays off
flow.x: A house at €200,000, a mortgage of €160,000 at 3.5% for 25 years. Purchase costs 8%, maintenance 1% a year, 2% return given up on the money tied up.

goals.label: With rent and prices flat, find after how many years buying costs less
goals.hint: Move only the years: purchase costs are paid just once.

goals.label: Now go back to 5 years and make buying pay off anyway
goals.hint: Over 5 years buying wins only if rent is high, or if the house rises in value.

flow.after: With these numbers it takes about 11 years for buying to beat rent of €800. Over a short time it wins only if rent is high or prices rise, and nobody has certainty about prices. Before the house, one thing has to be decided: how long you plan to stay in it.

flow.x:
The result changes a lot with three numbers. It helps to know in which direction they push.

• **The ratio of rent to price.** Rent of €800 a month on a house worth €200,000 amounts, over a year, to 4.8% of the price. Where rents are high compared with prices, buying pays for itself sooner.
• **The mortgage rate.** On €160,000 of debt, each extra point is about €1,600 more interest a year.
• **How long you stay.** It is the number that counts most, and it is the only one that depends only on you.

Then there is what no calculation measures: the stability of a home of your own, or the freedom to change city without having to sell. They have a value, but not the same for everyone. The calculation is there to tell you how much you are paying for them.

flow.q: An apartment costs €180,000. The same apartment rents for €750 a month. What is a year's rent as a percentage of the price?
flow.exp: A year's rent is \(750 \times 12 = \text{€}9{,}000\). Compared with the price: \(\dfrac{9{,}000}{180{,}000} =\) **5%**. The higher this number, the sooner buying pays for itself.

lessons.note: Buying has costs that don't come back: purchase, interest, maintenance. They are paid back only with time. The right question is after how many years.

ex.q: Which of these home-buying expenses is not recovered when you sell?
options: The part of the payment that repays principal
The taxes and legal fees paid at purchase
ex.exp: The down payment and the principal repaid stay inside the value of the house: you get them back when you sell. Taxes, legal fees and agent are paid once and don't come back.

ex.q: You plan to stay in a city for two years. What usually costs less?
ex.exp: In two years the purchase costs don't have time to spread out. Buying would pay off only if prices rose a lot in the meantime, and that can't be known beforehand.

ex.q: How is mortgage interest like rent?
options: It is collected by whoever sold you the house
It is the price for using money that isn't yours, and it doesn't come back
ex.exp: With rent you pay to use a house that isn't yours. With interest you pay to use money that isn't yours. In both cases it is a cost, not a saving.

lessons.title: How big a mortgage you can afford

flow.q: A couple earns €3,000 net a month between them. With a mortgage at 3.5% for 25 years, how much can they borrow without exceeding a prudent payment?
flow.after: The most widely used rule says the payment shouldn't exceed **a third of income**: here €1,000 a month. At 3.5% for 25 years, a €1,000 payment repays a mortgage of about **€200,000**. The third isn't a law: it is the margin you need to withstand an unexpected expense without missing a payment.

flow.x:
**How big a mortgage you can afford isn't decided by the price of the house: it is decided by the payment you can handle.**

The Bank of Italy indicates as reasonable a payment that doesn't exceed **one third of disposable income**. Inside that third must also fit the payments you already have: the car, a loan, a payroll-deduction loan (the Italian cessione del quinto).

Once the payment is fixed, the mortgage depends on two things.

• **The term.** More years means more mortgage with the same payment, but much more interest.
• **The rate.** Each extra point reduces the mortgage that the same payment can repay.

Then there is a second limit: as a rule the bank lends up to **80% of the value** of the house. The rest, plus the purchase costs, has to come from your savings.

flow.t: How big a mortgage an income can carry
flow.x: The payment is a third of net income. Move income, rate and term.

goals.label: Reach a mortgage of at least €190,000
goals.hint: You can raise income, lengthen the term or lower the rate.

goals.label: Now get €190,000 paying less than €80,000 in interest
goals.hint: A long term raises interest. Try fewer years and more income, or a lower rate.

flow.after: Lengthening the term makes the mortgage grow, but also the interest bill. If it takes 30 years and a payment at the limit to reach the price, the signal is a different one: that house costs too much for that income.

flow.t: How the bank looks at you
flow.x:
To decide, the bank looks at four things.

• **Income, and how stable it is.** A permanent contract counts for more than a fixed-term one.
• **The debts you already have**, and how you paid them: it checks the credit databases.
• **The value of the house**, estimated by its own appraiser. What counts is the appraisal, not the price you agreed.
• **How much you put in yourself.**

If you choose an adjustable rate, run a test on your own: does the payment hold up with two points more? On €160,000 over 25 years, going from 3.5% to 5.5% takes the payment from €801 to €983 a month.

flow.q: Marta and Luca earn €3,300 net a month together and already pay €250 a month for the car. With the one-third rule, what mortgage payment can they add?
flow.exp: A third of income: \(\dfrac{3{,}300}{3} = \text{€}1{,}100\). The car payment has to fit inside it too: \(1{,}100 - 250 =\) **€850**.

lessons.note: Payment within a third of income, counting other debts. The bank usually lends up to 80% of the appraised value. A longer term means more mortgage, but more interest.

ex.q: Net income of €2,700 a month, no other debts. What is a prudent mortgage payment?
ex.exp: A third of income: \(\dfrac{2{,}700}{3} =\) **€900**. With €1,350 half of the income would be committed: one unexpected expense would be enough to cause trouble.

ex.q: With the same payment, what happens if you lengthen the mortgage from 20 to 30 years?
options: You get more mortgage, and pay more interest in all
You pay less interest in all
ex.exp: With more years the same payment repays a bigger debt. But interest is paid for ten more years, and its total goes up a lot.

ex.q: You agreed on a price of €200,000, but the bank's appraiser values the house at €185,000. On which figure does the bank calculate the 80%?
options: On the average of the two figures
ex.exp: The bank lends based on the value estimated by its appraiser. 80% of €185,000 is €148,000: to reach the price you need €52,000 of your own, not €40,000.

lessons.title: GDP, inflation, unemployment

flow.q: Out of 100 Italians between 15 and 64, 63 have a job. Of the other 37, how many count as unemployed in the statistics?
flow.after: About **4**. The other 33 don't work but aren't looking for a job either: they study, take care of the home, have stopped looking. The statistics call them **inactive**. For ISTAT, the Italian statistics institute, only someone who has no job, is looking for one and is ready to start counts as unemployed. And the unemployment rate is calculated only on those who work or look: 4 out of 67, that is about 6%.

flow.t: GDP, and how to read it
flow.x:
**GDP is the value of everything a country produces in a period: goods and services, from bread to doctor visits.**

When a news story says GDP has grown, look at three things.

• **Compared with when.** The change on the previous quarter is called quarter-on-quarter; the one on the same quarter a year ago, year-on-year. In summer 2026 Italian GDP was flat on the previous quarter and 0.8% higher than a year earlier.
• **Real or nominal.** Nominal GDP rises even just because prices rise. Real GDP strips out inflation: it is the number the news reports.
• **Total or per person.** A country can grow just because it has more inhabitants. For the standard of living, **GDP per capita** counts.

Real growth is obtained, more or less, like this:

$$\text{real} \approx \text{nominal} - \text{inflation}$$

And one limit: GDP measures how much is produced, not how people live. It doesn't say how income is divided, and it doesn't count unpaid work.

flow.q: In one year a country's nominal GDP grows 3.5% and prices grow 2.7%. By roughly how much did real GDP grow?
flow.exp: \(\text{real growth} \approx \text{nominal growth} - \text{inflation} = 3.5\% - 2.7\% =\) **0.8%**. The rest of the growth is made only of higher prices.

flow.x:
You have already met inflation: it is the general rise in prices. In the news it comes with three labels.

• **Year-on-year**: this month's prices against those of the same month a year ago. It is the number in the headlines.
• **Month-on-month**: against last month. It tells whether the run is accelerating or slowing down.
• The **shopping basket**: only food and household and personal care products. These are everyday purchases, so it is the increase you feel the most.

A real example: in October 2026 ISTAT estimated +5.4% year-on-year and +0.9% on the month, with the shopping basket at +2.5%. Energy prices were the ones driving it.

A frequent trap: if inflation falls from 5% to 3%, prices do not fall. They still rise, only more slowly.

flow.t: A hundred people and a rate
flow.x: A hundred people between 15 and 64. Whoever is not employed and not looking for work is inactive.

goals.label: Bring unemployment below 5% without creating jobs
goals.hint: If the employed stay at 63, only the number of people looking can change.

goals.label: Now create three jobs
goals.hint: Raise the employed to 66 and see what the two rates do.

flow.after: The unemployment rate counts only people looking for work. If someone stops looking they become inactive, and the rate falls even if nobody found a job. That is why it has to be read together with the employment rate, which tells how many people actually work.

items: Works part-time, 20 hours a week
For the statistics, having worked at least one hour in the week is enough.
Without a job, sends out résumés every week
Does not work, is looking and is available: unemployed.
Studies and is not looking for work
Does not work and is not looking: for the statistics, among the inactive.
Has stopped looking: thinks they will not find anything
Whoever no longer looks does not count among the unemployed.
On Italy's wage supplement fund for a month
Whoever is absent from work for a short time stays among the employed.

lessons.note: GDP: check whether it is real and compared with when. Lower inflation doesn't mean lower prices. Unemployment counts only those who look: read it together with employment.

ex.q: A country's real GDP grows 0.5% and its population 1%. What happens to GDP per capita?
ex.exp: GDP grows less than the population: the share that on average falls to each person shrinks by about half a percentage point.

ex.q: Inflation goes from 5% to 2%. What do prices do?
options: They go back to the level of a year earlier
They still rise, but more slowly
ex.exp: Lower inflation means prices that rise less quickly. For prices to fall you need negative inflation, which is called deflation.

ex.q: In one month the unemployment rate falls, but the number of employed doesn't rise. What may have happened?
options: Some people stopped looking for work
ex.exp: Whoever stops looking goes from unemployed to inactive, and drops out of the count. The rate falls even if nobody found a job.

lessons.title: Deficit and public debt

flow.q: In 2025 the Italian state spent more than it took in. By how much, for every €1,000 of GDP?
flow.after: **€31** for every 1,000 of GDP, that is 3.1%: it is the **deficit**. It seems little, but it adds to a debt that is already worth €1,367 for every 1,000 of GDP. The deficit is what is missing in one year. The debt is what has piled up over all the past years.

flow.x:
**The deficit is how much the state spends over what it takes in during a year. Public debt is the sum of past deficits, still to be repaid.**

One is measured over a year, the other builds up over time.

To cover the deficit the state borrows money, by selling securities such as BOT and BTP, the Italian government bonds. Every year that ends in deficit adds debt.

Both numbers are measured relative to GDP, because what matters is the size of the debt compared with the economy that has to carry it.

| | Italy, 2025 | EU threshold |
|---|---|---|
| Deficit | 3.1% of GDP | 3% |
| Debt | 136.7% of GDP | 60% |

Whoever exceeds a 3% deficit can end up in a European procedure, which asks for a plan to get back in line. Italy has been in one since 2024.

items: How much the state spends over what it takes in this year
It is the result of a single year.
All the BOT and BTP still to be repaid
It is what the state has to repay in all.
The European reference is 3% of GDP
The 3% concerns each year's deficit.
The European reference is 60% of GDP
The 60% concerns the accumulated debt.
It grows every year in which the accounts close in the red
Every deficit adds to the debt.

flow.t: What makes debt rise or fall
flow.x:
The ratio of debt to GDP can fall even without repaying €1. It depends on three forces.

• **Interest** makes debt grow, because it has to be paid every year. In 2025 Italy paid €87 billion: 3.8% of GDP.
• **Growth** makes GDP grow, that is the number under the fraction. What counts is nominal growth, prices included.
• The **primary balance**: the difference between revenue and spending before paying interest. If it is positive it is called a primary surplus, and it reduces debt. In 2025 Italy's was 0.8% of GDP.

The rule is this: if the rate paid on the debt is higher than growth, debt rises on its own, and to stop it you need a primary surplus. If growth exceeds the rate, debt falls on its own.
We start from numbers close to Italy's 2025 figures: debt at 137% of GDP and deficit at 3.1%.

sliders.label: Average rate paid on the debt
Primary balance, as a share of GDP

goals.label: Bring debt below 130% of GDP
goals.hint: You can raise growth, lower the rate or raise the primary balance.

goals.label: Now do it with growth of 1%
goals.hint: With little growth you need a big primary surplus, or a lower rate.

flow.after: If growth stays at 1% and the rate stays at 3%, to get below 130% you need a primary surplus of 3.5% of GDP every year, for ten years: more taxes or less spending by tens of billions. With growth of 3.5% half a point would be enough. That is why, when talking about debt, growth counts as much as cuts.

flow.q: A country has debt equal to 140% of GDP and pays an average of 3% interest. How much does it spend on interest each year, as a percentage of GDP?
flow.exp: \(\text{interest} = \text{debt} \times \text{rate} = 140\% \times 3\% =\) **4.2%** of GDP. It is money that every year cannot go to schools, healthcare or pensions.

lessons.note: The deficit is for one year, the debt piles up. Both are measured against GDP. Debt falls if growth exceeds the rate paid, or with a primary surplus.

ex.q: A country ends the year with a lower deficit than the year before. What happens to its debt?
options: It still rises, but less than before
ex.exp: As long as the accounts close in deficit, the amount of debt keeps rising. A smaller deficit only means it rises more slowly.

ex.q: What is a primary surplus?
options: Revenue higher than spending, before paying interest
The debt left over at the end of the year
ex.exp: The primary balance compares revenue and spending without counting interest on the debt. When it is positive it is called a primary surplus: it is the resources left to pay interest and reduce debt.

ex.q: A debt costs 3% on average and nominal GDP grows 5%. With a balanced primary balance, what does the ratio of debt to GDP do?
ex.exp: Debt grows 3% because of interest, but GDP grows 5%: the fraction shrinks. That is why growth, even growth made of inflation, lightens debt.

lessons.title: Spread and rating

flow.q: November 2011, in the middle of the debt crisis: the spread between BTPs and Bunds hits its record. How many basis points?
flow.after: **574 basis points**, on November 9, 2011: to lend money to Italy for ten years the market asked 5.74% more than for Germany. On November 10, 2026 the spread was at 102. That number is a thermometer: it tells how risky lending to one state is considered compared with another.

flow.x:
**The spread is the difference between the yield on ten-year Italian government bonds, the BTPs, and that on German bonds, the Bunds.**

It is measured in **basis points**: 100 basis points are one percentage point.

$$\text{spread} = \text{BTP} - \text{Bund}$$

Germany is the benchmark because its bonds are considered the safest in the euro area. The **spread** is therefore the premium the market asks for lending to Italy instead of Germany.

Why it ends up in the news:

• if it rises, the state pays higher interest on new bonds, and that money leaves the public budget;
• over time the rates that banks charge on mortgages and loans rise too;
• whoever already holds BTPs sees their price fall.

flow.q: On November 10, 2026 the ten-year BTP yielded 4.27% and the Bund 3.25%. What was the spread, in basis points?
flow.exp: \(\text{spread} = 4.27\% - 3.25\% = 1.02\%\). One percentage point is 100 basis points, so the spread was **102 basis points**.

flow.t: The rating: the report card of debt
flow.x:
A **rating** is a grade on the ability of a state, or of a company, to repay its debts. It is given by private agencies: the most followed are S&P, Moody's and Fitch.

The scale goes from AAA, the top, down to D, which means a missed payment. The line that matters is in the middle.

| Band | S&P grades |
|---|---|
| Investment grade | AAA to BBB− |
| Speculative | BB+ and below |

Many funds can only buy **investment grade** securities. Whoever falls below that line loses some of its buyers, and pays higher rates.

At the beginning of November 2026 Italy has BBB+ from S&P and from Fitch, and Baa2 from Moody's, which on its scale equals BBB: a few notches above the line.

Next to the grade there is the **outlook**: positive, stable or negative. It says in which direction the grade could move.

items: AAA
A
BBB
BB
CCC
flow.x: Tap the grades from the highest to the lowest.
flow.after: From BBB up we are in the investment grade band. From BB down, in the speculative one. Inside each letter there are then pluses and minuses: BBB+ is one notch above BBB.

lessons.note: The spread is the extra yield of BTPs over Bunds, in basis points. The rating is the grade on the debt: from BBB− up it is investment grade, below it is speculative.

ex.q: The spread goes from 80 to 150 basis points. What does it mean?
options: That the market asks more to lend to Italy instead of Germany
That BTPs yield less than Bunds
ex.exp: A wider spread means that the yield on BTPs has moved further from that on Bunds: to buy Italian bonds the market wants a higher premium.

ex.q: You hold a BTP bought a year ago. The spread rises a lot, with German yields unchanged. What happens to the price of your bond?
ex.exp: If the spread rises with Bund yields unchanged, the BTP yield has risen. Bonds already in circulation, which pay lower coupons, are worth less. If you hold it to maturity you still receive all the principal.

ex.q: A country goes from BBB− to BB+. Why is it important news?
options: Because only the name of the grade changes
Because it leaves the investment grade band
ex.exp: BBB− is the last notch of investment grade. With BB+ you enter the speculative band: many funds can no longer hold those bonds and have to sell them.

lessons.title: Stock market indexes

flow.q: The FTSE MIB is the most quoted index of the Italian stock market. How many companies does it contain?
flow.after: There are **40**: the largest and most traded of those listed in Milan. An index is not the whole stock market: it is a basket chosen by a rule. The American S&P 500 contains 500, the German DAX 40.

flow.x:
**A stock market index sums up in a single number the prices of a group of stocks. If it rises, on average those stocks are worth more.**

Its value is expressed in points, but points alone say nothing: what counts is the percentage change, calculated like this:

$$\frac{\text{today} - \text{yesterday}}{\text{yesterday}}$$

Each index tells a different piece of the market.

• The **FTSE MIB**: 40 large Italian companies, among which banks and energy weigh a lot.
• The **S&P 500**: 500 large American companies, among which technology weighs a lot.

When you hear that the stock market has wiped out billions, it means the market value of companies has fallen. No cash has vanished: the prices at which those stocks trade have fallen. They can rise again, or fall further.

flow.q: An index closes at 40,600 points. The day before it had closed at 40,000. By what percentage did it rise?

flow.x:
In most indexes the companies don't count the same: each weighs in proportion to its value on the stock market, its **market capitalization**.

A company worth 100 billion moves the index ten times more than one worth 10 billion.

Two consequences.

• A few names can decide the day. In the FTSE MIB, in mid-2026, the top five companies alone were worth more than half of the index.
• The index can rise even if most of the stocks fall: it is enough that the biggest ones rise.
Three companies: the large one weighs 60, the medium one 30, the small one 10. Move their daily changes.

goals.label: Make the index rise 3% with the medium and small ones flat or down
goals.hint: Just move the largest company.

goals.label: Now make the index close down with two out of three companies up
goals.hint: Make the large one fall, and the other two rise a little.

flow.after: The large company alone is worth 60% of the index: if it rises 5%, the index rises 3% with the others flat. And a day with two stocks out of three up can close in the red. The index tells how the market is doing on average, weighted by value. It doesn't tell how most of the companies are doing.

flow.x:
• **Dividends are not visible.** Almost all the indexes quoted in the news track only prices. Whoever held the stocks also collected the dividends: over many years, the real return is higher than the one the index shows.
• **Points are misleading.** A drop of 500 points is serious on an index at 5,000 and almost nothing on one at 50,000. Always look at the percentage.

And remember that an index is not the economy. Inside it there are only listed companies, often large and with a lot of business abroad: the stock market can rise in a year when GDP is flat.

lessons.note: An index is a basket of stocks weighted by market value: look at the percentage, not the points. It usually doesn't count dividends. And the stock market is not the whole economy.

ex.q: An index loses 400 points. What do you need to tell whether it is a lot or a little?
options: The value it started from, to calculate the percentage
The number of companies it contains
ex.exp: Four hundred points are 4% of an index at 10,000 and 0.8% of one at 50,000. Without the starting value the number says nothing.

ex.q: In an index weighted by market capitalization, which company moves the result the most?
options: The one with the most employees
The one worth the most on the stock market
ex.exp: The weight of each company is in proportion to its market value. The largest count more, and can decide the direction of the day on their own.

ex.q: The FTSE MIB rises 1%. What can you say for sure?
options: That, taking the weights into account, its 40 companies are on average worth more
That all Italian stocks have risen
That the Italian economy has grown 1%
ex.exp: An index tells how its basket did on average, weighted by value. Some companies may have fallen, those outside the basket don't count, and the stock market is not GDP.
